questions.question: At 02:10 you page the on-call L2 analyst about a confirmed high-severity alert, as your playbook requires. Ten minutes pass with no reply. What should you do next?

options.text: Keep the alert open and hand it to the morning shift with a note that L2 did not answer
Start containment yourself on the affected server, since nobody senior is available
Page again and, if the agreed wait time passes, escalate to the next on-call level (for example the IR manager)
Post the full alert details in the company-wide IT chat channel so that whoever happens to be awake can pick it up quickly

explanation.correct: An escalation procedure says how long to wait for a response and what to do when nobody answers. The usual pattern (described in the earlier NIST guide, SP 800-61r2) is to repeat the first contact, wait a short defined time, then go one level up, for example to the IR team manager, and keep going up until someone takes ownership. Record every attempt with its time so the delay is explained in the incident record.

distractors.a: Parking a confirmed high-severity alert for hours lets the attacker keep working; an unanswered page is exactly the case the escalation chain exists for.
distractors.b: Acting outside your playbook and authority on a server can destroy evidence or break a business service; L1 escalates, it does not take decisions reserved for L2/L3.
distractors.d: Broadcasting incident details to a wide audience breaks need-to-know and can tip off an insider; escalation goes to named people in the on-call chain.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that escalation is a defined procedure with time limits, not a single phone call.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2 (superseded by r3), section 3.2.6 on escalation when there is no response
NIST SP 800-61r3 Incident Response Recommendations

questions.question: You are an MSSP analyst on a client's major-incident bridge. The client's IT manager tells you to reimage an infected server now; ten minutes earlier the client's security manager told you to keep it running for evidence collection. Neither of them is the designated incident commander. What do you do?

options.text: Follow the IT manager, because reimaging restores the client's service fastest and the business is waiting
Take the conflict to the incident commander on the bridge, act on their decision and log it
Follow whichever instruction came first and ignore later ones
Do both: take a quick snapshot of the disk yourself, then reimage without telling anyone

explanation.correct: A major incident has one incident commander (incident lead) who owns decisions and assigns tasks, so conflicting orders from other managers go back to that person instead of being settled by the analyst. You state the conflict on the bridge, act on the commander's decision and log who decided what and when. For an MSSP this is also contractual: the client's agreed contacts and the incident commander define who may authorise a destructive action such as a reimage.

distractors.a: Seniority or speed of recovery does not give someone authority over the response; a reimage destroys evidence the security manager may need, and that trade-off is the commander's call.
distractors.c: Order of arrival is not authority; the later instruction may reflect new information, and either way the conflict stays unresolved.
distractors.d: A destructive action without a decision or a record breaks role clarity and leaves no trace of who authorised it; a rushed, undocumented snapshot is also weak evidence.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know who you take instructions from during a major incident and how to handle conflicting orders.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, roles, responsibilities and authorities (GV.RR-02)

questions.question: During an outage of the bank's mobile app, a journalist calls your personal mobile and asks whether customer data was stolen. You are an L1 analyst working on the incident. What is the right response?

options.text: Decline to comment, refer them to the bank's press contact and tell your incident lead about the call
Confirm only what is already public, so that the story is accurate
Say that no customer data was stolen, to prevent panic among customers and protect the bank's reputation
Decline and hang up, and mention the call to nobody so as not to draw more attention to the incident

explanation.correct: Media contact during an incident goes through a designated point of contact (with a backup) who has been briefed with Legal and Communications, so the bank speaks with one consistent voice. An analyst does not comment, redirects to that contact and reports the call so it is logged; the call is itself useful information, because it may mean details of the incident are already leaking.

distractors.b: Even 'public' facts become an insider's statement on the record, and you do not know what has been officially said or what is legally sensitive.
distractors.c: An unverified reassurance may be false and later contradict the official statement and the regulatory notifications.
distractors.d: Declining is right, but hiding the contact loses a signal the incident lead and Communications need; contacts with outside parties should be documented.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know who is allowed to speak for the organisation during an incident.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2 (superseded by r3), section 2.3.4 on communicating with the media and outside parties
NIST SP 800-61r3, incident response reporting and communication (RS.CO)

questions.question: While triaging, you find an email from a criminal group threatening to publish stolen company data unless a ransom is paid. A colleague suggests calling the police cybercrime unit right away. What is correct?

options.text: Call the police cybercrime unit yourself right now, because a crime has been committed and reporting it should not wait for internal approvals
Reply to the sender and ask for proof of the stolen data before involving anyone
Delete the email so that staff do not see it and panic
Preserve the email and escalate to the incident lead; police contact is made by designated people under the IR plan

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 recommends notifying law enforcement and regulators based on criteria in the incident response plan and with management approval, through designated individuals. Legal is usually involved because the contact has consequences for evidence handling, disclosure and any decision about the ransom demand. The analyst's job is to preserve the email with its full headers and escalate it immediately as a high-priority finding.

distractors.a: The intent is good, but an individual analyst calling the police commits the organisation without approval and can clash with how Legal handles the case; the plan names who makes that call.
distractors.b: Engaging the extortionist is a decision for the incident lead, Legal and management; an analyst's reply can escalate the situation and reveal what the organisation knows.
distractors.c: Deleting the email destroys evidence of the extortion, including the headers needed to investigate it.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.CO-02 (notifying law enforcement and regulators)

questions.question: You are escalating a suspected account compromise from L2 to the IR lead. Which escalation note is the most useful?

options.text: 'Probable APT intrusion targeting the finance file server, most likely the same group that hit us last year. I recommend shutting down the whole finance VLAN immediately. I will send logs and evidence once I finish the full investigation tomorrow.'

'jdoe: sign-in from 203.0.113.45 08:12 UTC (new country, MFA approved by phone); external forwarding rule 08:20 UTC. Confirmed: 14 mails forwarded. Unknown: how MFA was approved, other accounts. Done: rule exported, nothing changed. Need: decision on revoking sessions.'
A 40 MB export of every sign-in log in the tenant for the last 30 days, attached without comment
'jdoe looks compromised, please check.'

explanation.correct: A good escalation lets the receiver decide quickly: timestamps in one time zone with their sources, the affected user and assets, what is confirmed versus unknown, what has already been done (and that nothing destructive was done) and the decision that is needed. Note b gives the IR lead exactly that in a few lines; the inbox forwarding rule is a known collection technique (MITRE T1114.003).

distractors.a: It leads with an unverified attribution and a drastic recommendation and holds back the evidence the lead needs to judge it.
distractors.c: Raw data without a summary pushes the analysis back onto the IR lead and delays the decision; evidence supports a summary, it does not replace it.
distractors.d: Too little: no timestamps, indicators, scope or requested decision, so the lead has to start the investigation again.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can separate confirmed facts from hypotheses and ask for a specific decision when you escalate.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, incident escalation and elevation (RS.MA-04)
MITRE ATT&CK T1114.003 Email Forwarding Rule

questions.question: Which three kinds of entry belong in the incident record so that a reviewer can later reconstruct and defend the response? Choose three.

options.text: The analyst's personal opinion about the suspected employee's character
Each action taken, with who did it and a timestamp that includes the time zone
Decisions such as isolating a host, with who approved them and when
A single summary note written at closure, which keeps the ticket short and avoids recording half-checked facts
Each contact with outside parties (vendor, police, regulator): when, with whom, what was shared

explanation.correct: The record must let someone rebuild the response step by step: timestamped actions with their actor, decisions with their approver, and all contacts with outside parties, which NIST recommends documenting for liability and evidence purposes. Handlers record facts as they happen; interpretation belongs in the report, clearly labelled as such. NIST SP 800-61r3 also asks that the integrity and provenance of these records be preserved.

distractors.a: Incident logs should hold facts, not personal opinions or conclusions; subjective remarks about a person may later be disclosed to the employee, a court or a regulator and weaken the case.
distractors.d: Writing only at closure loses detail and exact times; every step from detection to resolution should be documented and timestamped as it happens.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2 (superseded by r3), section 3.2.5 Incident Documentation
NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.AN-06 (records of investigation actions)

questions.question: You promised business stakeholders an incident update every two hours. At the next slot, the investigation has found nothing new. What do you do?

options.text: Send it on time: no material change, what is in progress, decisions needed, next update time
Skip this update and send the next one only when there is real news, to avoid flooding busy stakeholders with noise
Fill the update with preliminary hypotheses so that it does not look empty
Ask stakeholders to read the incident ticket themselves from now on

explanation.correct: A fixed cadence builds trust only if it is kept. Silence is read as loss of control or bad news and triggers ad-hoc calls that interrupt the responders. A short 'no material change' update still gives current status, work in progress, decisions needed and the next update time; if the cadence should change (for example from two to four hours once the incident is stable), say so explicitly. NIST SP 800-61r3 expects procedures that define what is reported to whom and when, including regular status updates.

distractors.b: Missing a promised update creates uncertainty and pulls stakeholders onto the bridge to ask for news, which slows the response.
distractors.c: Unverified hypotheses in a stakeholder update tend to be repeated as facts and may later have to be retracted, sometimes in front of a regulator.
distractors.d: Tickets are written for responders and can contain sensitive details; pushing stakeholders to them breaks the agreed communication plan.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.CO-02 (what is reported to whom and when)

questions.question: A relationship manager who resigned last week uploaded 300 client files from her corporate laptop to a personal cloud storage account over two evenings. Her line manager wants to email her today and ask her to explain. What should the investigation do first?

options.text: Let the line manager send the email, since a quick explanation may close the case
Disable her account and collect the laptop from her desk first thing this morning, before she can upload anything else
Ask her colleagues informally whether she mentioned taking work home or moving to a competitor
Stop the email, preserve logs and device evidence, and agree with HR and Legal when she is interviewed

explanation.correct: Any contact before the evidence is secured can tip her off, and she could delete the cloud copies or the local traces. The investigation first preserves what it needs (audit and DLP logs, endpoint telemetry, a forensic copy of the laptop under chain of custody) and agrees with HR and Legal how and when she is interviewed and when her access changes, so that the employment process and any legal action rest on sound evidence. Interim controls against further uploads can be agreed in the same discussion.

distractors.a: An email asking for an explanation is the classic tip-off: it gives her time to delete evidence and prepare a story before anything is preserved.
distractors.b: An immediate, visible account disable and laptop seizure without HR and Legal can breach the employment procedure and does not recover the cloud copies; it may be right later, as an agreed step.
distractors.c: Informal questions spread the suspicion, damage her privacy if she is innocent, and are likely to reach her quickly.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand tipping off and why evidence comes before confronting an insider.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, roles: human resources and legal
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: Your insider-risk process shows triage analysts pseudonymised identities (for example 'User-7F3A') until a case is opened. An alert shows User-7F3A downloading far more HR files than their peers. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Triage the behaviour against peers and, if it meets case criteria, open a case so an authorised investigator can reveal the identity
Ask an administrator to tell you who User-7F3A is, so you can judge whether the person is trustworthy before spending time on triage
Close the alert, because analysts are not allowed to investigate pseudonymised users
Post the alert in the SOC chat and ask whether anyone recognises the pattern from a colleague

explanation.correct: Pseudonymisation lets analysts judge behaviour on evidence without bias and without exposing employees' identities more than needed. The identity is revealed only when the activity justifies a case, by people with the right role, through a logged process. Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management, for example, pseudonymises users by default and relies on role-based access and audit logs for exactly this reason.

distractors.b: Looking up the identity outside the process defeats the privacy control and invites bias; whether someone 'seems trustworthy' is not evidence.
distractors.c: Pseudonymisation does not block the investigation; it controls when, and by whom, the identity is revealed.
distractors.d: Sharing the alert widely breaks need-to-know and may reach the person concerned or their colleagues.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Plan for Insider Risk Management (privacy by design, pseudonymisation, stakeholders)

questions.subtopic: MSSP handoffs and authority to act
questions.question: At 03:00 your MSSP SOC sees ransomware precursors (credential dumping, then remote service creation) on a client's file server. The contract says server isolation needs approval from a named client contact and lists no pre-authorised server actions. The primary contact does not answer. What do you do?

options.text: Phone down the client's escalation list (secondary contact, duty manager), log each attempt and recommend isolation with evidence
Isolate the server now, because in an emergency the MSSP's duty of care overrides the contract
Email the findings to the primary contact and mark the ticket as 'client notified'
Wait until the client's business hours, since server actions out of hours carry an outage risk

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 notes that the contract should define the provider's authority to act on the organisation's behalf, including limits on operational decisions such as shutting down services to contain an incident. So the right move is to reach someone who can decide, fast: follow the client's escalation list in order, through channels that get an answer at 03:00, record each attempt and make a concrete recommendation backed by evidence. The gap (no pre-authorised server containment) belongs in the post-incident review so the contract and runbook allow defined emergency actions next time.

distractors.b: Acting beyond the agreed authority can cause an outage the client never accepted and exposes the MSSP to liability; emergency actions work only when they were pre-authorised.
distractors.c: An email at 03:00 is not an escalation; 'client notified' is false comfort while the attacker moves toward encryption.
distractors.d: Ransomware precursors are time-critical; waiting hours without trying the rest of the escalation list leaves the client exposed.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand that an MSSP's power to act comes from the contract, and how to escalate quickly within it.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, section 2.2 (third parties, division of responsibilities and authority to act)

questions.question: A DLP alert suggests that a spreadsheet with customer data was emailed to the wrong external recipient. Put the bank's handling steps in the correct order.

options.text: Assess, with the DPO, the likely risk to the affected customers: no risk, risk or high risk
Route the alert to the person responsible for breach handling and open the incident record with the detection time
Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of awareness if there is a risk, and inform customers if the risk is high; otherwise document why no notification is needed
Run a short initial investigation to establish with reasonable certainty whether personal data was compromised, and record that moment as the time of awareness

explanation.correct: The EDPB guidelines describe this flow: security events go to a person responsible for handling them; a short initial investigation establishes with a reasonable degree of certainty whether personal data was compromised, which is when the controller becomes 'aware' and the 72-hour clock starts; the likely risk to individuals is then assessed; finally the bank notifies the supervisory authority if there is a risk and informs the data subjects without undue delay if the risk is high. Under article 33(5) every breach is documented, including the reasoning when it is not notified, and the EDPB recommends involving the DPO promptly and throughout.

references.title: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification under GDPR
GDPR Article 33

questions.question: If an incident is very unlikely to lead to prosecution, such as a routine malware infection, the data collected during the response no longer needs integrity protection or a record of who handled it.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. NIST SP 800-61r3 notes that formal chain-of-custody procedures might not be applied to every incident, but collected incident data is still evidence and its integrity and provenance should be preserved. Cases also change: a 'routine' infection can turn out to involve an insider, a disciplinary process or a regulator's question. NIST SP 800-86 adds that when it is unclear whether evidence needs preserving, it should generally be preserved by default (hashes, restricted storage, a simple handling record).

distractors.a: Prosecution is only one use of evidence; disciplinary action, regulator inquiries, insurance claims and root-cause analysis all depend on data whose integrity you can demonstrate.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.AN-07 (integrity and provenance of incident data)
NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

questions.question: Two hours into a suspected data theft from the bank's card-processing environment, you prepare the first update for the executive committee. Which three elements belong in it? Choose three.

options.text: What is confirmed so far and what is still unknown, stated separately
Impact on customers, operations and regulatory duties, including which notification clocks may be running
The list of indicators of compromise (hashes, IP addresses, domains) found so far
Actions under way, decisions needed from the committee, and the time of the next update
The likely threat actor behind the attack, based on the analyst's first impression of the malware and its infrastructure

explanation.correct: Executives must make decisions, so the update gives them facts with their confidence (confirmed versus unknown), the business and regulatory impact including any GDPR or DORA clocks that may be running, what is being done, what they must decide and when the next update comes, in short business language. NIST SP 800-61r3 recommends updating senior leadership regularly on the status of major incidents.

distractors.c: Indicators matter to responders and threat intelligence, not to an executive decision; they lengthen the update without helping anyone decide.
distractors.e: Unverified attribution in a board-level message is likely to be repeated as fact; attribution belongs in an update only when it is supported and relevant to a decision.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.CO-03 (regular updates to senior leadership)

questions.question: You lead the response to an intrusion at a bank. The attacker is active on two servers, and the threat intelligence team wants to delay containment for 48 hours to watch the attacker in a monitored environment and learn their tools. What must happen before you agree?

options.text: Nothing beyond your own approval, since containment timing is a technical decision for the IR lead
The communications team must first prepare a public statement in case the attacker notices
Consult Legal and get the accountable risk owner's documented decision, since a deliberate delay lets the attacker keep escalating
Have the threat intelligence team confirm they will monitor around the clock, which is enough to accept the risk

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 notes that redirecting an attacker to a sandbox to observe them delays containment and eradication, that the IR team should first discuss the strategy with the legal department, and that the intentional delay is dangerous because the attacker could escalate access or compromise other systems. In a bank the decision also affects customer harm and regulatory reporting, so it belongs to the accountable risk owner with Legal's input, recorded together with the risks accepted.

distractors.a: Accepting a known, ongoing risk to customer data and services is a business and legal decision, not only a technical one.
distractors.b: A public statement does nothing to manage the legal and operational risk of the delay and would be premature.
distractors.d: Round-the-clock monitoring reduces the risk but does not remove it, and it does not answer the legal and accountability questions.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you see that some response choices need legal and business sign-off, not just technical judgement.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.MI (incident mitigation, R1 on observing the attacker)

questions.question: A SaaS company has a multi-hour outage caused by a security incident. Match each audience with what its updates should focus on.

right.text: Tasks, owners, indicators and containment status
Business impact, risk, decisions needed and the next update time
What customers are experiencing, workarounds and a holding script for calls, without internal investigation details
Confirmed impact on the service, what customers should do, and when the next update will be posted
Full forensic timeline with attacker IP addresses and details of the exploited vulnerability

explanation.correct: Each audience gets what it needs to act: leadership decides on risk and resources, support staff answer callers consistently, responders coordinate technical work, and customers learn the impact and what to do. NIST SP 800-61r3 separates incident coordination (among responders), notification and public communication. The full forensic detail (r5) belongs to no external audience during the incident; NIST's media guidance warns against revealing technical details that could help other attackers.

distractors.l4: Publishing forensic details (r5) can help other attackers and may contradict findings that are still changing; customers need impact and actions.
distractors.l2: Support staff need a script for callers, not the responders' task list (r1); giving them internal details invites leaks.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.CO (four categories of incident communication)
NIST SP 800-61r2 (superseded by r3), section 2.3.4.1 The Media

questions.subtopic: insider suspected inside the IR team
questions.question: At a software vendor, evidence in an open case suggests that one of your own SOC engineers used privileged access to read customer data without a ticket. That engineer is currently assigned to the case. How do you proceed?

options.text: Keep the engineer on the case so they suspect nothing, and quietly review their work
Ask the engineer in the team stand-up to explain the access, to keep things transparent
Tell the whole SOC about the suspicion so that everyone double-checks the engineer's actions and nothing else slips through unnoticed
Move the case to a need-to-know group without the engineer, involve HR and Legal, and use independent forensics

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-86 says that when an incident is suspected to involve a member of the incident handling team, an independent party (another team or an external firm) should perform the forensic work. The suspect must lose access to the case records, which hold the evidence against them, so the case moves to a restricted group; NIST SP 800-61r3 notes that incident records can name users who acted inappropriately and must be access-controlled. HR and Legal are involved because this may become a disciplinary or legal matter, and the customer data involved may trigger notification duties.

distractors.a: Leaving the suspect on the case lets them see what is known and alter or delete evidence and records.
distractors.b: Public questioning tips them off, harms them if they are innocent, and bypasses the HR and Legal process.
distractors.c: Broadcasting a suspicion breaks need-to-know, damages the person's privacy and makes witness accounts less reliable.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can handle a conflict of interest inside your own team without compromising evidence or fairness.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
NIST SP 800-61r3, RS.AN-06 (safeguarding incident records)

questions.subtopic: evidence handoff between MSSP and forensics firm
questions.question: Your MSSP has just acquired a disk image from a client's laptop and must hand it to the external forensics firm the client has hired. Put the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Hand over the media with a chain-of-custody form signed and timed by both the releasing and the receiving person
The forensics firm makes a working copy, verifies its hash and analyses only the copy
Compute and record the SHA-256 hash of the image immediately after acquisition
The forensics firm recomputes the hash of the received image, confirms it matches and records where the evidence is stored
Seal the media in tamper-evident packaging and log the item: identifiers, collector, date and time with time zone, seal number

explanation.correct: Integrity is fixed first with a hash at acquisition. The item is then sealed and logged with its identifiers, the collector and the time including the time zone. NIST SP 800-61r2 says evidence must be accounted for at all times and that every transfer is documented on a form signed by each party. The receiver proves nothing changed in transit by recomputing the hash and records the storage location, and analysis is done only on a verified working copy, as NIST SP 800-86 recommends.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2 (superseded by r3), section 3.3.2 Evidence Gathering and Handling
NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

questions.question: You review this chain-of-custody record before your MSSP's forensic report goes to the client's Legal team. Which two problems weaken the record? Choose two.
questions.context:
CHAIN OF CUSTODY - evidence item E-0142
Item: forensic image of laptop SSD, asset tag FIN-LT-0387 (client CL-207)

#  Date/time             Action                           By          SHA-256 (first 12)
1  2026-03-04 09:12 UTC  Image acquired, hash computed    A. Ionescu  7d3f9a0c21be
2  2026-03-04 09:40 UTC  Sealed in bag S-55812            A. Ionescu  -
3  2026-03-04 14:05      Released to courier              A. Ionescu  -
4  2026-03-05 10:30 UTC  Received, seal S-55812 intact    M. Varga    -
5  2026-03-05 11:02 UTC  Hash recomputed on receipt       M. Varga    7d3f9a0c21be
6  2026-03-06 16:20 UTC  Working copy created             M. Varga    7d3f9a0c21be
7  2026-03-07 08:15 UTC  Keyword search run on original   M. Varga    -

options.text: Entry 5 shows exactly the same hash as entry 1, which suggests the value was copied over rather than actually recomputed
Entry 3 has no time zone and names no courier or receiver, leaving the image unaccounted for overnight
The record uses UTC instead of the client's local time
Entry 7 shows analysis run on the original image instead of the working copy
Entry 6 should not exist, because making a working copy breaks the chain of custody

explanation.correct: A custody record must account for the evidence at all times: each transfer names who released it and who received it, with date, time and time zone and both signatures. Entry 3 hands the image to an unnamed courier at a time with no zone, leaving a gap until entry 4 that the other side can exploit. Entry 7 breaks the rule that examination is done only on a verified copy (NIST SP 800-86), even though a working copy existed. Matching hashes at entries 1, 5 and 6 are exactly what you want to see.

distractors.a: Identical hashes are the expected result of a correct recomputation; a different value would be the problem.
distractors.c: UTC is good practice for timelines; the issue is an entry with no time zone, not the choice of UTC.
distractors.e: Working copies are how analysis should be done; creating one with a matching hash is part of the chain, not a break in it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can spot the gaps a lawyer would attack in a custody record.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2 (superseded by r3), section 3.3.2 Evidence Gathering and Handling
NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

questions.subtopic: involving HR, Legal and the DPO
questions.question: A bank's DLP team confirms that an employee in the payments department forwarded customer statements to a personal address over three months. Before the investigation goes further, which three functions should be formally involved? Choose three.

options.text: Human Resources, because the outcome may be a disciplinary process that must follow employment rules
The employee's team members, who know the employee's habits best
Legal, to confirm which monitoring and evidence collection is lawful and to protect any later legal claim
The DPO or privacy function, since customer data left the bank and the inquiry processes employee data
Public communications, so that a press statement is issued before the media hears about the case from someone else

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 lists HR as a role when an employee is suspected of intentionally causing an incident, recommends notifying HR when malicious insider activity has occurred, and points responders to Legal when an incident may have legal consequences. The forwarded statements are also a likely personal data breach, so the DPO must assess the GDPR notification duty, and the EDPB recommends informing the DPO promptly and involving them throughout. The DPO also helps keep the employee investigation proportionate.

distractors.b: Team members are possible witnesses, not decision-makers; telling them spreads the suspicion and risks tipping off the employee.
distractors.e: Communications may need to be ready later, but a press statement at this stage is premature and could prejudice both the investigation and the employee's rights.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3, section 2.2 roles (Legal, Human Resources) and RS.CO-03
EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification (role of the DPO)

questions.question: Once a bank has notified the data protection authority of a suspected personal data breach, it cannot correct that notification: if forensics later shows that no personal data was accessed, the bank is still treated as having had a breach and may be penalised for over-reporting.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. The EDPB guidelines say a controller can update the supervisory authority if follow-up investigation shows the incident was contained and no breach actually occurred; the information is added and the incident is recorded as not being a breach, and there is no penalty for reporting an incident that turns out not to be a breach. That is why, under time pressure, notifying with the facts known and saying more will follow is safer than waiting for certainty past the 72 hours.

distractors.a: This belief pushes teams to delay notification until every fact is certain, which is the real compliance risk under article 33.

references.title: EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification under GDPR

questions.question: A bank becomes aware of an ICT incident on Monday at 09:00. At 20:00 the same day it classifies the incident as major under DORA. By when, at the latest, must the initial notification reach the competent authority?

options.text: Tuesday 09:00, 24 hours after the bank became aware of the incident
Monday 13:00, 4 hours after the bank became aware of the incident
Tuesday 00:00, 4 hours after classification
Thursday 20:00, 72 hours after classification

explanation.correct: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301, article 5, sets two limits for the initial notification: within 4 hours of classifying the incident as major, and no later than 24 hours after becoming aware of it. Both apply, so the earlier one binds: 20:00 plus 4 hours is Tuesday 00:00, before the 24-hour limit of Tuesday 09:00. In practice the bank's reporting path, including whoever approves the submission, must work at night.

distractors.a: The 24-hour limit is an outer cap; here the 4-hour limit from classification ends earlier and therefore binds.
distractors.b: The 4-hour limit runs from classification as major, not from awareness.
distractors.d: 72 hours is the clock for the intermediate report, and it runs from the initial notification, not from classification.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can apply two overlapping regulatory clocks correctly instead of reciting one number.

questions.question: A bank became aware of an incident on Monday at 09:00. Its first assessment did not meet the major-incident criteria. On Wednesday at 10:00, new data shows the thresholds are now met and the bank classifies the incident as major. When is the DORA initial notification due?

options.text: It was due on Tuesday at 09:00, so it is already late and must be sent with an explanation of the delay
Wednesday at 14:00, within 4 hours of the classification
Thursday at 10:00, within 24 hours of the classification
No initial notification is needed any more; the bank goes straight to the intermediate report

explanation.correct: Article 5(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301 covers this case: if the incident was not classified as major within 24 hours of awareness but is classified as major later, the initial notification is due within 4 hours of that classification. The bank should keep the earlier assessment and the new data that changed it in the incident record, because the authority may ask why classification came on Wednesday.

distractors.a: The 24-hour limit applies when the incident is classified within that window; for a later, documented classification the rule is 4 hours from classification.
distractors.c: No 24-hour window is counted from classification; after classification the clock is 4 hours.
distractors.d: Every major incident starts with an initial notification; the intermediate report follows within 72 hours of it.

questions.question: An incident takes down a bank's online banking, which supports a critical function, for 3 hours. Facts so far: 40 000 of 900 000 online-banking clients affected; affected transactions about 4 % of the daily average by number and value; no relevant clients or counterparts affected; one Member State; estimated costs 30 000 EUR; no data affected; no media coverage or complaints. How should it be classified under DORA on these facts?

options.text: Not major on these facts: only one materiality threshold (downtime) is met; reassess as facts change
Major, because downtime above 2 hours on a service supporting a critical function is enough on its own
Not major, because fewer than 10 % of clients were affected, and the client threshold must be met for every major incident
Major, because any incident that affects a critical service is major by definition

explanation.correct: Under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772, article 8, an incident is major when it affects critical services and either the threshold for successful, malicious, unauthorised access that may cause data losses is met, or two or more of the other materiality thresholds are met. Here only service downtime (more than 2 hours for an ICT service supporting a critical function) is met; clients (4.4 %, below 10 % and below 100 000), transactions, geographical spread, data losses and economic impact (below 100 000 EUR) are not. The classification and its reasoning go into the incident record and are reassessed: media coverage or repeated complaints would add the reputational threshold and make it major, and recurring incidents with the same apparent root cause can add up to a major one.

distractors.b: One threshold is not enough unless it is the malicious unauthorised access threshold; downtime alone does not make the incident major.
distractors.c: No single threshold is mandatory; the client threshold is one of several, and any two of them (with critical services affected) would make it major.
distractors.d: Affecting critical services is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one; the materiality thresholds must also be met.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can apply the DORA classification logic to facts instead of treating one big number as decisive.

questions.question: A bank has classified a data-theft incident as major and already sent its DORA initial notification to the financial supervisor. It is now 60 hours since the bank became aware that customer personal data was stolen, and forensics cannot yet say how many customers are affected. Legal proposes waiting for the exact number. What is correct?

options.text: The DORA notification already covers the breach, so no separate data protection notification is needed
Wait for the exact count, because an incomplete GDPR notification would itself breach article 33
Send a NIS2 early warning to the national CSIRT instead, since that regime covers cyber incidents
Notify the data protection authority within 72 hours with approximate figures and categories, and add details in phases

explanation.correct: GDPR breach notification is separate from DORA incident reporting: the DORA reports go to the financial competent authority, the GDPR notification to the data protection supervisory authority. Article 33(3) asks for the approximate number of data subjects and records, article 33(4) allows information in phases, and the EDPB says missing precise figures should not block timely notification. For a bank, DORA incident reporting applies in place of NIS2 reporting.

distractors.a: DORA and GDPR are different obligations to different authorities with different clocks; the EDPB reminds controllers that other notification duties come in addition to, and separate from, GDPR.
distractors.b: GDPR expressly allows approximate figures and phased information; waiting beyond 72 hours for precision is what creates the violation.
distractors.c: For financial entities, DORA takes precedence over NIS2 incident reporting, and a NIS2 early warning would not replace the GDPR notification anyway.

questions.question: An employee's laptop is stolen from a car. It holds a copy of a customer list. IT confirms that full-disk encryption was enabled, the laptop was shut down rather than asleep, the recovery key is held only in the central key store, and the data also exists on the file server. What is the correct notification decision?

options.text: Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours anyway, because any loss of a device that holds personal data must always be notified
Notify every customer on the list but not the supervisory authority, since the customers bear the risk
Notification is likely not required, but record the breach and the reasoning, and reassess if the key is compromised
Record nothing, because encrypted data is not personal data

explanation.correct: Losing a properly encrypted device is still a personal data breach, but if the key is intact and the device is not the only copy of the data, the data are in principle unintelligible to the thief and the breach is unlikely to result in a risk, so the EDPB says notification may not be needed. The details in the stem matter: the EDPB notes a device may be encrypted when switched off but not in standby. Article 33(5) still requires the breach to be documented with the reasoning for not notifying, and the decision must be revisited if the key or the encryption later proves compromised.

distractors.a: Article 33(1) exempts breaches unlikely to result in a risk to individuals; a securely encrypted device with an intact key is the EDPB's own example of such a case.
distractors.b: Telling data subjects is required only for high risk (article 34), and article 34(3)(a) exempts data made unintelligible by encryption; alerting customers while skipping the authority inverts the logic.
distractors.d: Encrypted personal data is still personal data and its loss is still a breach, which must be recorded under article 33(5) even when it is not notified.

questions.question: A payroll provider that processes a bank's employee data detects a breach on Monday at 08:00 and informs the bank on Wednesday at 10:00. In principle, when does the bank's 72-hour GDPR clock start?

options.text: Monday at 08:00, when the provider detected the breach, so the bank has about 22 hours left
When the bank's own forensic review has confirmed the provider's findings
It does not start, because as processor the provider must notify the authority itself
Wednesday at 10:00, when the provider informed the bank

explanation.correct: Article 33(2) requires the processor to notify the controller without undue delay, without first assessing the risk. The EDPB guidelines say the controller should in principle be considered aware once the processor has informed it, so the bank's clock starts on Wednesday at 10:00. The bank should still record the provider's delay, take it up under the contract (which can set an earlier notification deadline for the processor) and review its oversight of the provider.

distractors.a: The processor's detection is not the controller's awareness; the EDPB ties the controller's clock, in principle, to being informed by the processor.
distractors.b: The bank may investigate further, but being informed by its processor already makes it aware; waiting for its own confirmation eats into the 72 hours.
distractors.c: The legal duty to notify the supervisory authority stays with the controller; a processor may notify on its behalf only if authorised, and the responsibility remains the controller's.

questions.question: A bank's contract lets its MSSP prepare and submit DORA incident reports on the bank's behalf. For a major incident, the MSSP submits the initial notification three hours late. Who is accountable to the supervisor for the late report?

options.text: The bank, which stays fully responsible even when the task is outsourced
The MSSP, because the signed contract transferred the reporting obligation to it together with the task
Both equally, as joint reporting entities under DORA
Nobody, as long as the MSSP explains the delay in the report

explanation.correct: DORA article 19(5) lets financial entities outsource the reporting task to a third-party service provider, but the financial entity remains fully responsible for meeting the reporting requirements. GDPR follows the same logic: a processor may notify on the controller's behalf if authorised, but the legal responsibility stays with the controller. As an MSSP consultant, you design the service so that the client can oversee the deadlines, for example with a shared clock, an approval step and a fallback submitter.

distractors.b: A contract can move the work, not the legal obligation; the supervisor holds the financial entity accountable.
distractors.c: DORA does not create joint reporting entities; the MSSP's failure is a contractual matter between it and the bank.
distractors.d: Explaining a missed deadline to the authority is required, but it does not move accountability away from the bank.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that outsourcing a regulatory task does not outsource the responsibility.

questions.question: You work at a SaaS vendor that processes personal data as a processor for 40 business customers. You confirm that an attacker accessed a database shared by the tenants of 12 of those customers. What does GDPR require of the vendor now?

options.text: Assess the risk to individuals for each customer first, and notify only the customers whose breaches are likely to result in a risk
Notify each of the 12 affected customers without undue delay, with what is known now, and add details in phases
Notify the supervisory authority directly on behalf of all 12 customers, which discharges their obligations
Wait until the root cause and the full list of affected records are known, so that each customer gets one complete notification

explanation.correct: Under article 33(2) a processor must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a breach. The EDPB adds that the processor does not first assess the risk (that is each controller's job), that it should notify promptly and add information in phases so controllers can meet their 72 hours, and that when one incident affects several controllers it must report the details to each of them. Customer contracts may set tighter deadlines.

distractors.a: The risk assessment belongs to each controller; a processor that filters notifications by its own view of risk can make customers miss their 72-hour clock.
distractors.c: A processor may notify on a controller's behalf only if that controller authorised it, and even then the legal responsibility stays with the controller.
distractors.d: 'Without undue delay' does not allow waiting for the root cause; phased notification exists so that controllers learn early.

questions.question: Match each report with the event that starts its clock.

left.text: GDPR notification to the supervisory authority (within 72 hours)

right.text: Submission of the latest (updated) intermediate report
Classification of the incident as major (4 hours), and awareness of the incident (24 hours at the latest)
Submission of the initial notification
Submission of the incident notification (the 72-hour report)
Becoming aware of the personal data breach
Submission of the NIS2 early warning (the 24-hour report)

explanation.correct: DORA (Delegated Regulation 2025/301, article 5): initial notification within 4 hours of classification as major and no later than 24 hours after awareness; intermediate report within 72 hours of the initial notification; final report within one month of the latest (updated) intermediate report. NIS2 article 23: early warning within 24 hours and incident notification within 72 hours of awareness, final report within one month of the incident notification. GDPR article 33: within 72 hours of becoming aware, where feasible. For financial entities DORA takes precedence over NIS2, while GDPR runs in parallel whenever personal data is involved.

distractors.l1: The DORA initial notification has two clocks (r2): 4 hours from classification as major and, at the latest, 24 hours from awareness; neither the submission of another report nor the NIS2 early warning starts it.
distractors.l2: The 72-hour intermediate report runs from the submission of the initial notification (r3), not from classification or awareness, an error common in secondary summaries.
distractors.l3: The DORA final report runs from the latest (updated) intermediate report (r1); counting one month from the initial notification or from classification is wrong.
distractors.l4: NIS2's final report runs from the 72-hour incident notification (r4), not from the 24-hour early warning (r6); DORA's final report runs from the intermediate report instead.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know what starts each clock, which is where real reporting mistakes happen.

questions.question: You are estimating the economic impact of an incident for the bank's DORA classification (threshold: costs and losses above 100 000 EUR). Which three statements about what counts are correct? Choose three.

options.text: The cost of a new detection platform bought after the incident to prevent a recurrence is included
Overtime paid to IT staff during recovery is included
Fees for external forensic and legal advice engaged for the incident are included
Amounts expected from the insurer are deducted from the total
Compensation paid to customers for failed payments is included

explanation.correct: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772, article 7, counts direct and indirect costs and losses without accounting for financial recoveries, including staff costs such as overtime, advisory costs such as legal counselling and forensic services, and redress and compensation to customers (as well as expropriated funds, replacement of hardware or software, contractual penalties, forgone revenue and communication costs). It excludes costs to enhance the business after the incident, insurance premiums and normal running costs. Amounts not yet known are estimated, so management receives an estimate with its basis that is refined later.

distractors.a: Upgrades and improvements made after the incident are expressly excluded; they are investment, not loss caused by the incident.
distractors.d: Economic impact is assessed without accounting for financial recoveries, so expected insurance payouts are not deducted.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can build a defensible impact figure for management instead of a guess.

questions.question: A workstation is confirmed to be beaconing to a known command-and-control domain. Which action is a short-term containment step, as opposed to eradication or a long-term change?

options.text: Remove the malicious scheduled task and delete the binary it launches
Reimage the workstation from the standard corporate build
Network-isolate the workstation through the EDR agent
Redesign egress so that all internet traffic must pass an authenticating proxy

explanation.correct: Short-term containment is a fast, usually reversible action that stops the damage from growing while you investigate. EDR network isolation cuts the host off from the C2 server and from lateral movement but leaves it running, so memory and disk evidence stay intact and the isolation can be released later. NIST SP 800-61r2 lists the duration of the solution (emergency workaround, temporary workaround, permanent fix) among the criteria for choosing a containment strategy.

distractors.a: Removing the persistence and the binary is eradication. Done before containment and scoping, it destroys evidence and may miss other footholds.
distractors.b: Reimaging is eradication and recovery. It wipes the evidence you still need to scope the incident.
distractors.d: An egress redesign is a long-term hardening change that takes weeks; it does nothing to stop this host tonight.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can place an action in the right phase and explain why the quick, reversible step comes first.

questions.subtopic: blocking a destination vs isolating a host vs containing an identity
questions.question: A phishing email has already been purged from all mailboxes. Proxy logs show that 12 users opened its link to a fake sign-in page and 3 of them submitted the form. No file was downloaded and EDR is quiet. Which containment fits?

options.text: Network-isolate all 12 workstations through EDR and keep them isolated until each has had a full scan
Block the domain at the proxy and DNS; reset the password and revoke sessions for the 3 users who submitted
Reset passwords for all 12 users who opened the link and leave the domain reachable, since the email has been purged
Block the domain at the proxy only, because a password typed into a fake page is of no use without the user's device

explanation.correct: The risk sits in two places: the site itself (a forwarded copy or a saved link can still reach it) and the credentials the 3 users typed in. Blocking the destination closes the first for everyone with one change. Containing the 3 identities (password reset plus session revocation, then a check of their sign-in logs for use of the stolen password) closes the second. Nothing executed on the hosts, so host isolation adds disruption without removing the risk.

distractors.a: Over-containment: no payload ran and EDR is quiet, so isolating 12 hosts disrupts users while the stolen credentials stay usable.
distractors.c: Opening the page does not expose a password, so resetting all 12 is broader than needed, and leaving the site reachable keeps the door open through forwarded or saved links.
distractors.d: A stolen password is usable from any device unless MFA or Conditional Access stops it, so the 3 accounts still need containing.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you pick the containment lever (destination, identity or host) that matches where the risk actually is.

questions.question: At 03:00 the EDR in a bank's SOC flags active file encryption on a branch workstation. The runbook pre-authorises L1 analysts to network-isolate workstations that show ransomware behaviour. The on-call incident manager does not answer the first call. What should the L1 analyst do?

options.text: Wait for the incident manager to call back, because isolation is a business decision
Power off the workstation remotely, which stops the encryption faster than isolation
Phone the branch user to ask whether they opened anything unusual before acting
Isolate the workstation as the runbook allows, then keep escalating

explanation.correct: Pre-authorisation exists for exactly this case: the decision about workstations was taken in advance by whoever owns the risk, so the analyst acts at once and escalates in parallel. NIST SP 800-61r2 notes that containment decisions are much easier when strategies and levels of authority are set beforehand. Recording the isolation time and each escalation attempt feeds the incident timeline and any later regulatory report.

distractors.a: For workstations the decision was already made in the runbook; waiting lets the encryption spread to mapped shares.
distractors.b: Powering off loses volatile evidence (processes, network connections, possibly key material) and is not what the runbook authorises; EDR isolation stops the spread without that loss.
distractors.c: The user is unlikely to be reachable at 03:00 and the answer would not change the action; contact can follow containment.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that pre-approved actions are meant to be used without waiting, with escalation running alongside.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (sections 2.3.1 and 3.3.1)
MITRE ATT&CK T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact

questions.question: At a software company, a developer pushed a cloud access key to a public Git repository and, 10 minutes later, pushed a follow-up commit that deletes it. What containment step is required?

options.text: Revoke or rotate the key, then check the provider's logs for its use
Make the repository private so that the commit is no longer publicly visible to anyone
Rewrite the repository history so that the key no longer appears in any commit
Watch the key for misuse for a week and rotate it only if suspicious calls appear

explanation.correct: Once a secret has been public it must be treated as compromised: automated scanners harvest keys from public repositories, and clones, forks and cached views keep the commit even after a later commit deletes the file. GitHub's own guidance makes revoking or rotating the secret the first step, which may make rewriting history unnecessary. After rotation, the provider's audit trail (for example AWS CloudTrail filtered on the access key ID) shows whether anyone used the key during the exposure window.

distractors.b: Making the repository private hides it from now on but does nothing about copies taken during the exposure, and the key still works.
distractors.c: Rewriting history does not reach copies already cloned, forked or cached, and the key stays valid until it is revoked.
distractors.d: Waiting leaves a known-exposed credential live; misuse may also be quiet (enumeration, creating new keys) and easy to miss.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat an exposed secret as compromised and contain the credential, not the file.

questions.question: Once a compromised host has been network-isolated through the EDR agent, malware already running on that host can no longer cause damage on it.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. Network isolation cuts the host off from other systems and from its command-and-control channel, but processes already running locally keep running: an encryptor can keep encrypting local disks, and NIST SP 800-61r2 warns that some malware reacts to lost connectivity by overwriting or encrypting the host's data. Isolation must therefore be followed by stopping the malicious process (for example an EDR stop-and-quarantine action) and by watching the isolated host, not by assuming it is safe.

distractors.a: Isolation limits spread and remote control, not local execution; treating it as complete containment is how local data is lost after the network is cut.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand what isolation does and does not stop.

questions.subtopic: isolating a host vs disabling an account vs blocking a destination
questions.question: An MSSP analyst is handling four client incidents. Match each situation to the containment lever that addresses it most directly.

left.text: A phished password is used from an unfamiliar country for webmail and VPN; the user's laptop shows no malicious activity
Commodity malware on 40 workstations beacons to one newly registered domain
An attacker runs tools interactively on one server under a local admin account they created there
A partner integration's API key is pulling customer records from an unknown IP address

right.text: Revoke or rotate the key and review everything it accessed
Block sign-in, revoke sessions and reset the password for the account
Network-isolate the host through the EDR agent and keep it powered on
Block the destination at DNS and the web proxy while the hosts are scoped and cleaned
Power off every affected machine to stop all activity at once

explanation.correct: Contain where the attacker's access lives. In l1 the access is the identity, so isolating the laptop would not stop sign-ins from the attacker's own device; block sign-in, revoke sessions and reset the password. In l2 one destination serves all 40 hosts, so a single DNS and proxy block cuts the C2 for every one of them while you clean. In l3 the access lives on the server itself (a local account and tools), so isolating the host stops it while keeping memory for forensics. In l4 the access is a credential tied to no person or device, so the key is revoked or rotated and its activity reviewed to scope what was taken.

distractors.l1: Isolating the user's laptop does nothing here: the attacker signs in from their own device with the stolen password.
distractors.l2: Isolating 40 workstations is possible but slower and more disruptive; the shared C2 destination is the common point to cut first.
distractors.l3: Powering off would stop the attacker but destroys memory evidence of their tools; EDR isolation achieves the cut-off without that loss.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you choose containment by where the access lives rather than by habit.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.1)

questions.question: A bank's payment reconciliation server shows an active command-and-control beacon. The forensics team wants a full memory capture before anything changes; the service owner wants the server shut down now. EDR is installed and healthy. Which approach serves both needs?

options.text: Shut the server down now; a disk image taken afterwards will hold everything the investigation needs
Leave it connected until the memory capture finishes, so that the attacker does not notice the response
Network-isolate it through EDR, then capture memory over the EDR channel
Reimage it straight away from the gold build so that the reconciliation service is back as fast as possible

explanation.correct: EDR network isolation cuts the server off from the attacker and the rest of the network but keeps it powered on and connected to the EDR service, so memory capture, live response and a triage package can still be collected. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, for example, documents that isolation retains connectivity to its service, and its investigation package includes active network connections and the DNS cache. Containment and evidence preservation stop being a trade-off. The order of volatility still applies: memory and live state first, disk afterwards.

distractors.a: Shutdown destroys volatile evidence (running processes, injected code, live connections) that a disk image cannot recover.
distractors.b: Tip-off concerns are real, but leaving an active C2 channel open on a payment system for the length of a capture gives the attacker time to act; isolation keeps the evidence anyway.
distractors.d: Reimaging before collection wipes the evidence needed to scope the intrusion and to know whether other systems are affected.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know modern EDR isolation removes the old choice between pulling the plug and keeping the evidence.

questions.subtopic: disabling external sharing in a data-leakage case
questions.question: At an insurer, a DLP alert shows that an employee created an 'Anyone' sharing link on a OneDrive folder with 400 claim files containing health data and emailed the link to a personal address. The employee is on leave today. What is the right first containment step?

options.text: Remove the Anyone link, then check the audit log for uses of it
Delete the folder and its files so that nothing more can be downloaded through any link that may exist
Leave the link in place until the employee returns from leave and can explain the business reason
Block the personal email domain on the mail gateway so that the link cannot be sent there again

explanation.correct: The exposure is the live link: anyone holding the URL can open the files without signing in, so removing it (logged as AnonymousLinkRemoved) stops further access at once without touching the data. The audit log then scopes what already happened: AnonymousLinkCreated shows when the link was made and AnonymousLinkUsed records anonymous access through it, including the IP address. In Microsoft Sentinel: OfficeActivity | where Operation in ('AnonymousLinkCreated', 'AnonymousLinkUsed'). Health data is special-category data, so the findings go to the DPO for the GDPR breach assessment (72 hours from awareness).

distractors.b: Deleting destroys business records and evidence; removing the link closes the exposure without that loss.
distractors.c: The link stays usable by anyone who has it while you wait; the explanation can come after containment.
distractors.d: The link was already delivered; blocking future mail does not revoke it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you contain the exposure path (the link) rather than the data or the person, and know which audit events scope it.

questions.subtopic: credential reset for a service account
questions.question: During a bank intrusion, the attacker used the domain service account svc_recon, which 12 scheduled jobs across several servers use, including month-end payment batches. The attacker's last use was two weeks ago; a coordinated eviction is planned for Saturday. How should the svc_recon password reset be handled?

options.text: Reset it right now without telling the job owners, because every hour the old password works adds risk
Disable the account permanently and let the job owners raise tickets when their scheduled jobs start failing
Leave the password unchanged for now, because resetting it would break the month-end payment batches
Map every system that uses the credential, then reset it in the Saturday window, update each one and watch for failures

explanation.correct: A service-account reset is containment with a business blast radius: every job that stores the old password fails after the reset. Mapping the consumers first (scheduled tasks, services, application configuration, scripts) lets you update them in the same window as the coordinated eviction, so the attacker loses the credential and the payment batches keep running. Failed logons for svc_recon afterwards (Event ID 4625 on the host where the attempt is made) show either a forgotten consumer or someone still trying the old password; the source host tells you which. Longer term, a managed service account removes the manual rotation problem.

distractors.a: An unplanned reset breaks month-end jobs and, ahead of the planned eviction, warns the attacker; with no use for two weeks, the planned window is the better trade-off.
distractors.b: Disabling breaks the same jobs without a plan to replace the credential, causing an outage the business did not approve.
distractors.c: A credential known to the attacker cannot stay valid; the business impact is handled by planning the reset, not by skipping it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can contain a credential without causing an outage the business never agreed to.

Add the domain to the email gateway's blocklist so that no message can reference it
Block the domain at the DNS resolver and web proxy, and alert on hosts still trying it

explanation.correct: On shared infrastructure the IP address is not unique to the attacker, so the domain name is the precise indicator: a DNS block (sinkhole or protective DNS) plus a proxy block on the hostname stops the beacon for every infected host without breaking other services on the same CDN. Alerting on hits turns the block into a detection for infected hosts not yet found. Know its limits: malware that uses hard-coded IPs or encrypted DNS can bypass a resolver block, which is why the proxy rule and host cleaning still matter.

distractors.a: The shared CDN address also serves legitimate sites, including the client's HR platform, and the attacker can move to another CDN address at any time.
distractors.b: Blocking a whole provider causes a broad outage to stop one malicious hostname.
distractors.c: The beacon is HTTPS traffic from the hosts, not mail, so an email blocklist does not touch it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you weigh collateral impact and indicator precision when choosing where to block.
