NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.1)

questions.question: During a client incident, your MSSP applied 14 emergency firewall and DNS blocks and isolated 3 hosts. The client is now moving to recovery. What should happen to these emergency changes?

options.text: Leave all of them in place permanently, because extra blocks can only improve the client's security
Remove all of them when the incident is closed, so that the environment returns to its original state
Review each with the client: make needed ones permanent via change control, remove the rest
Leave them for the client's firewall team to sort out later, because the MSSP's role ended at containment

explanation.correct: Emergency containment changes are workarounds with an intended duration; NIST SP 800-61r2 distinguishes emergency workarounds, temporary workarounds and permanent solutions when choosing a containment strategy. At recovery each change needs a decision: keep it as a permanent, owned change through the client's change process (for example a block on confirmed attacker infrastructure), or remove it once the reason is gone (an isolated host that has been rebuilt). Recording the outcome in the incident record keeps the client's rule base explainable and auditable.

distractors.a: Unowned emergency rules pile up, break legitimate traffic later and are not understood by anyone at the next audit.
distractors.b: Blanket removal can reopen paths the attacker used, such as blocks on confirmed C2 infrastructure.
distractors.d: Handing over without a list leaves the client unable to tell emergency rules from intended ones; closing them out is part of the engagement.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat containment changes as something to manage to closure, not fire and forget.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.1)

questions.question: An attacker had SYSTEM-level control of a file server for six days. Antivirus has since quarantined their backdoor DLL and no alerts have fired for 48 hours. The server owner asks to return it to service after one more clean scan. What do you recommend?

options.text: Rebuild from a known-good image and reset the credentials used on the server
Restore the whole server from last night's backup, because it is the most recent complete copy
Return it to service once a second full scan with updated signatures comes back clean
Remove the DLL's registry references, delete the attacker's account and keep the server in place

explanation.correct: With SYSTEM rights for days, an attacker can change almost anything (services, scheduled tasks, WMI subscriptions, drivers, local accounts, credentials in memory), so removing what you happened to find cannot prove a clean state. Rebuilding from a known-good image is the reliable path; data is restored separately after checks, the exploited weakness is fixed so the attacker cannot simply return, and credentials that touched the server are reset because they may have been harvested. Cleaning in place can be acceptable for low-privilege commodity malware with a well-understood footprint, not here.

distractors.b: Last night's backup falls inside the six-day dwell time, so it can bring the same persistence back into production.
distractors.c: A clean scan shows only that known signatures are absent; it cannot prove there is no persistence the scanner does not recognise.
distractors.d: Removing the known pieces leaves whatever else the attacker changed; with SYSTEM rights that list is open-ended.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you tie the rebuild-or-clean decision to the attacker's privilege level and dwell time.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.4)
CISA #StopRansomware Guide (containment and eradication)

questions.question: A bank's IR lead is preparing the eradication sign-off after an intrusion that used two stolen accounts and a scheduled-task backdoor. Which THREE checks belong in the validation? (Choose 3.)

options.text: Close the eradication phase once the originally infected host has raised no new alert for 24 hours
Sweep every host, not only the known ones, for the indicators and the scheduled-task technique
Confirm both accounts were reset and sessions revoked, and that later sign-ins look legitimate
Treat the restored business services starting and running normally as proof that the attacker is gone
Keep the attacker-specific detections at raised priority for an agreed period

explanation.correct: Validation tries to prove the negative across the whole estate, not on the host you started with. A sweep for the indicators and for the technique itself (for example scheduled tasks created outside change windows, Event ID 4698) finds footholds the first analysis missed. Reviewing the reset accounts' sign-ins confirms the reset took effect (in Microsoft Sentinel, SigninLogs filtered on the two UserPrincipalName values since the reset time). Raised monitoring follows because, as NIST SP 800-61r2 notes, a resource that was attacked once is often attacked again.

distractors.a: No alerts on one host says nothing about the other hosts or about quiet persistence that does not alert.
distractors.d: A service starting shows availability, not that the attacker's access is gone; a restored system can run normally with a backdoor inside.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you validate eradication with evidence across the estate rather than by the absence of alerts.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.4)
MITRE ATT&CK T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task

questions.question: Put these steps for handling a single compromised workstation in the correct order.

options.text: Reconnect the rebuilt workstation and watch it under raised monitoring for the incident's indicators
Capture memory, then acquire a disk image, recording hashes and chain-of-custody details
Network-isolate the workstation through the EDR agent
Reimage from the known-good build and apply current patches
Verify the rebuild: EDR agent reporting, no indicator hits, and the weakness the attacker used is fixed

explanation.correct: Isolation comes first because it stops spread and remote control while keeping the machine running. Evidence is collected next, in order of volatility (memory before disk), because the rebuild will destroy it. Only then is the machine reimaged from a known-good build. The rebuild is verified before reconnection so that the gap the attacker used is not reconnected with it, and the host returns under raised monitoring because recurrence is common in the weeks after an incident.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3)

questions.question: A software company confirms that a Microsoft 365 user account is compromised: the attacker added their own authenticator app and an inbox forwarding rule. Put the containment and recovery steps in order.

options.text: Reset the password and have the user re-register MFA through a verified channel
Block sign-in for the account
Remove the attacker's authenticator method, the forwarding rule and any app consents found in scoping
Unblock sign-in and watch the account's sign-in logs for the attacker's IP addresses and devices
Revoke all of the user's sessions and refresh tokens

explanation.correct: Blocking sign-in first stops new authentication; revoking sessions and refresh tokens next stops tokens already issued from being renewed (Microsoft notes an existing access token stays valid until it expires, by default one hour, unless the app supports continuous access evaluation). This is the order in Microsoft's emergency revocation guidance. With the attacker locked out, their persistence is removed: the rogue authenticator would let them pass MFA again, and the forwarding rule keeps leaking mail without any sign-in. Only then does the user get a new password and re-register MFA, and the account returns under watch.

references.title: Microsoft Entra ID: revoke user access in an emergency
Microsoft Defender for Office 365: responding to a compromised email account

questions.question: Which TWO statements correctly describe how containing a data-leakage incident differs from containing an active ransomware outbreak at a bank? (Choose 2.)

options.text: In both cases the first containment step is always to network-isolate the user's workstation through EDR
Data that has already left cannot be pulled back, so leakage containment closes the exit channel and scopes what left
An insider leak is often contained with HR and legal, timed to avoid alerting the person; active encryption is contained at once
Leakage incidents need no regulatory notification assessment, because no system was damaged or made unavailable
Ransomware containment should wait until a full disk image of every affected host has been taken for evidence

explanation.correct: The goals differ. Ransomware attacks availability, so speed decides how many systems you lose and isolation is worth its disruption. Leakage attacks confidentiality: the copy outside is beyond host containment, so the work is to shut the exit path, scope exactly what left (audit logs, DLP incidents, proxy records) and handle the human side carefully, because an insider who notices early may delete traces or speed up. Either can trigger notification: a leak of customer data is a personal data breach to assess under GDPR art. 33 whether or not any system was harmed.

distractors.a: Leakage often runs through cloud services reachable from any device, so isolating one workstation may close nothing; the lever is usually the account, link or destination.
distractors.d: GDPR art. 33 is about the risk to individuals from the data, not about damage to systems; a leak of customer data needs the assessment.
distractors.e: Imaging every host first lets the encryption spread; CISA's guide puts isolating impacted systems first and speaks of imaging a sample of affected devices, not all of them.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can explain why one playbook does not fit both confidentiality and availability incidents.

references.title: CISA #StopRansomware Guide (detection and analysis, containment)
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR)

questions.question: A client receives an extortion email with 20 sample files from its HR file share; nothing is encrypted. EDR shows that rclone ran last week on a jump server under an IT admin account, uploading to a cloud storage provider. What should containment focus on?

options.text: Restore the HR share from backup to undo whatever changes the attacker made to the files on it
Close the access path (jump server and admin account) and preserve its evidence to scope exactly what was taken
Reply to the extortion email to buy time before taking any action that the attacker might be able to notice
Block the cloud storage provider company-wide and close the incident, since the upload channel is gone

explanation.correct: In theft-only extortion nothing needs restoring: the harm is the copy outside and the access that made it. Containment targets the path the attacker used (isolate the jump server, disable and reset the admin account, look for other accounts and tooling such as the rclone configuration file, which names the remote destination), while preserving the jump server's evidence so legal and the DPO learn which records left. Any contact with the extortionist is a decision for leadership and legal with specialist advice, not a first containment step.

distractors.a: The share was copied, not altered; a restore does not undo the theft and can overwrite evidence of what was accessed.
distractors.c: Engaging the extortionist contains nothing and is a leadership and legal decision; the attacker may still have access meanwhile.
distractors.d: Blocking the provider removes one exfiltration channel, but the access through the account and jump server remains and the stolen data is not yet scoped.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you recognise that data-theft extortion is contained at the access path, not through backups.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
CISA #StopRansomware Guide (signs of data exfiltration)

questions.question: A bank restored its payments-reconciliation database from the last clean backup, taken 20 hours before the outage. Eradication has been validated. Before the business owner signs off the return to service, which check confirms that the business can rely on the restored data?

options.text: Confirm that the database service starts and that users can log in to the application
Reconcile the restored data with the ledger and scheme records for the 20-hour gap
Run another full antivirus scan of the database server and attach the clean report to the sign-off
Ask the backup vendor to certify that the backup job completed without errors on that night

explanation.correct: A restore from a backup taken 20 hours earlier means everything processed in those 20 hours is missing from the database. Recovery validation for a financial system therefore includes reconciliation against independent records (core ledger, payment-scheme or counterparty files) and controlled replay or re-entry of the gap, with the business owner signing off on the result. NIST SP 800-61r2 describes recovery as restoring systems to normal operation and confirming they function normally; for a bank, normal includes complete and correct balances.

distractors.a: Availability is necessary but proves nothing about the 20 hours of transactions missing from the restore.
distractors.c: Malware scanning is an eradication check, already done; it says nothing about missing transactions.
distractors.d: A successful backup job shows the copy was written correctly at that time, not that the data after the restore point is complete.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you see recovery as a business-integrity question, not only a technical restart.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.4)

questions.question: An attacker had access to a user's cloud mailbox for three days. You have blocked sign-in, revoked sessions and reset the password; EDR on the user's laptop shows nothing. Which THREE attacker changes must you look for and remove so that access or data flow does not continue? (Choose 3.)

options.text: Inbox rules and mailbox forwarding that send, move or delete messages
The messages in Sent Items from those three days, so that the attacker's emails are gone
Authentication methods the attacker registered, such as a new authenticator app or phone number
OAuth consent grants given to applications during the compromise window
The laptop's operating system, by reimaging it before the user signs in again

explanation.correct: Each of the three survives a password reset: forwarding and inbox rules keep copying or hiding mail without any sign-in (ATT&CK T1114.003), a rogue authenticator lets the attacker pass MFA again (T1098.005), and a consented OAuth app holds its own grant to the mailbox (T1528). Microsoft's guidance for a compromised account includes reviewing registered MFA devices and removing suspicious forwarding and inbox rules; it also notes that app passwords are not revoked by a password reset, so check those too.

distractors.b: Sent items are evidence: you need them to identify and warn recipients of fraudulent emails. Deleting them removes no access.
distractors.e: The compromise was of a cloud identity and EDR shows nothing on the laptop; reimaging adds cost without removing any cloud-side foothold.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know which footholds survive a password reset in a cloud mailbox compromise.

references.title: Microsoft Defender for Office 365: responding to a compromised email account
MITRE ATT&CK T1114.003 Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule

questions.question: At 14:00 on a weekday, EDR shows ransomware staging (credential dumping, a PsExec push being prepared) on one server in a bank's card-authorisation cluster. Isolating it will stop card authorisations until failover completes, about three hours. The playbook does not pre-authorise isolation of this cluster. How should the isolation decision be made?

options.text: The on-duty L2 analyst isolates at once, because security always takes priority over availability
The infrastructure team decides, because they own, patch and operate the servers in the cluster
The incident manager takes the recommendation and impact estimate to the decision-maker the plan names for the service
The bank first asks its competent supervisory authority for guidance before touching a critical payment system

explanation.correct: Taking a critical service down is a business-risk decision, so it belongs to the authority the incident or crisis plan assigns for that service (service owner, crisis lead or executive on call), informed by security's recommendation and IT's impact estimate. NIST SP 800-61r2 asks organisations to define levels of authority in advance precisely so that this happens in minutes, not hours. The record matters: a deliberate multi-hour outage of a critical service feeds the DORA major-incident classification (duration and service downtime are criteria) and the reports that follow. The same plan should state what happens if encryption actually starts, for example immediate isolation.

distractors.a: Without pre-authorisation, an analyst taking a payment system offline for hours makes a business decision they do not own, however strong the security case.
distractors.b: Infrastructure owns the technology but not the business risk of stopping card payments; they advise on failover time.
distractors.d: Regulators receive reports; they do not approve containment, and waiting for them costs time the attacker uses.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know who owns a containment decision with business impact and how to get it made fast.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (sections 2.3.1 and 3.3.1)
Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA)

questions.question: Your IR consultancy is engaged by a client where a targeted actor has held domain-level access for weeks. The actor is quietly collecting data; no destructive activity is seen and monitoring is in place. The client's IT team wants to reset each compromised account the moment you identify it. What do you advise?

options.text: Finish scoping under monitoring, then evict in one coordinated move, ready to act early if needed
Block all known C2 addresses today so the actor loses control, and plan the credential resets for next month
Take no containment action at all until the full forensic report is complete in a few weeks' time
Agree with IT, because every hour that a known compromised account stays active adds risk to the client

explanation.correct: Against an actor with domain-level access, piecemeal resets tip them off while leaving other ways in: they switch to other credentials, create new ones or forge tickets. The joint advisory AA20-245A (CISA and partners) lists preemptive credential resets and preemptive blocking of adversary infrastructure among common incident-handling mistakes for this reason. A coordinated eviction (credential resets including KRBTGT, C2 blocks and persistence removal at the same moment) removes all known access at once so the actor cannot pivot, and the agreed trigger keeps the option to act immediately if behaviour changes, for example signs of ransomware staging.

distractors.b: Blocking infrastructure first is another early warning, and C2 infrastructure is cheap to replace; a month between the blocks and the resets gives the actor time to regroup.
distractors.c: Waiting weeks with no plan leaves the actor collecting data; scoping should drive a planned eviction, not replace it.
distractors.d: Each visible reset tells the actor they are detected while they still hold other accounts; they adapt before you finish.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand tipping-off risk and why evicting a capable actor must be coordinated.

references.title: CISA AA20-245A: Technical Approaches to Uncovering and Remediating Malicious Activity
MITRE ATT&CK T1078.002 Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts

questions.question: After a domain admin compromise, the IR lead suspects the attacker extracted the KRBTGT account's hash. The recovery plan resets the KRBTGT password twice, with a wait between the resets. Why?

options.text: The first reset changes the password only on the PDC emulator; the second pushes it to the other domain controllers
The first reset can produce a weak password, so the second one makes sure a strong password is in place
Back-to-back resets are the documented procedure; a wait is needed only in forests with read-only domain controllers
One reset leaves the previous key valid for forged tickets; the wait lets legitimate tickets expire

explanation.correct: Microsoft's forest recovery guidance states that the KRBTGT password history holds the two most recent passwords, so after a single reset the old key is still there and a golden ticket forged with it can still be accepted; the second reset clears it. The same guidance says to wait 10 hours between resets, the default maximum lifetime for user and service tickets, so that tickets issued before the first reset expire normally instead of failing. Teams sometimes accept a faster second reset in an emergency, knowingly trading authentication disruption for speed; that is a deliberate decision, not the default.

distractors.a: Both resets are ordinary password changes that replicate to all writable domain controllers; the second reset is not about replication.
distractors.b: The system generates a strong KRBTGT password regardless of what the administrator types in the dialog.
distractors.c: Microsoft's procedure explicitly requires the wait for writable domain controllers; resetting back-to-back invalidates legitimate tickets and causes authentication failures.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand why golden tickets survive a single reset and the trade-off in timing the second one.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: AD forest recovery, reset the krbtgt password
MITRE ATT&CK T1558.001 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

questions.question: A bank's payment reconciliation server was restored after a ransomware incident. What do these records show, and what should happen next?
questions.context:
Investigation timeline (confirmed)
2026-02-27 21:40  first malicious logon to PAY-RECON-02, account svc_backup, source 198.51.100.23
2026-03-01 02:13  PAY-RECON-02 EventID=4698 TaskName=\UpdChk SubjectUserName=svc_backup (task action: C:\ProgramData\upd\updchk.exe)
2026-03-13 01:05  encryption starts on file servers

Recovery log, PAY-RECON-02
2026-03-15 09:12     restored from backup set of 2026-03-12 23:00, reconnected to production VLAN
2026-03-15 09:15:02  EventID=4688 NewProcessName=C:\ProgramData\upd\updchk.exe ParentProcessName=C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe
2026-03-15 09:15:04  firewall action=allow src=PAY-RECON-02 dst=203.0.113.77:443

options.text: updchk.exe is started by svchost.exe, so it is a Windows component; the outbound call is an update check and can be closed as benign
The connection is leftover traffic from the encryption phase and will stop once the EDR finishes its post-restore scan
The backup kept the attacker's persistence: isolate again, rebuild from a known-good image and reset svc_backup
Block 203.0.113.77 at the firewall and keep the server in production, since the encryption binary is not on the restored image

explanation.correct: The scheduled task was created on 1 March and the backup was taken on 12 March, so the backup faithfully preserved the backdoor: three minutes after reconnection the task's binary starts (Task Scheduler launches tasks under svchost.exe, which is why the parent looks normal) and calls out to 203.0.113.77. A clean restore point must predate the initial access (27 February), not just the encryption; when no such backup exists, rebuild from a known-good image and restore only application data after checking it. svc_backup created the task, so it is a compromised credential to reset, and restores should land in an isolated recovery network until validated, as CISA's guide advises to avoid reinfection.

distractors.a: svchost.exe is the normal parent for anything Task Scheduler launches, malicious tasks included; the binary path matches the task the attacker created on 1 March.
distractors.b: Encryption ended on 13 March; this is a new process starting after the restore and opening a fresh outbound connection, which is persistence, not residue.
distractors.d: Blocking one address treats a symptom: the backdoor keeps running and the attacker can switch infrastructure, the 'whack-a-mole' pattern CISA warns about.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you check a restore point against the intrusion timeline, not only the encryption date.

questions.question: At a SaaS company, an exposed IAM user access key was deactivated at 10:41. What explains the activity at 10:55, and what must containment add?
questions.context:
CloudTrail (simplified), account 111122223333, S3 data events enabled
10:02:11 CreateUser        caller=ci-deployer  key=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE  src=203.0.113.9  newUser=svc-metrics-ro
10:02:40 CreateAccessKey   caller=ci-deployer  key=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE  src=203.0.113.9  forUser=svc-metrics-ro
10:03:05 AttachUserPolicy  caller=ci-deployer  key=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE  src=203.0.113.9  user=svc-metrics-ro  policy=AdministratorAccess
10:41:30 UpdateAccessKey   caller=cloud-admin  src=10.20.1.15  target=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE  status=Inactive
10:55:12 ListBuckets       caller=svc-metrics-ro  key=AKIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE  src=203.0.113.9
10:55:48 GetObject         caller=svc-metrics-ro  key=AKIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE  src=203.0.113.9  bucket=example-customer-exports

options.text: Key deactivation takes up to an hour to propagate, so the old key is still being honoured; wait and check again
The exposed key created a new admin user with its own key; contain that user and everything the old key made
CloudTrail delivers events late and out of order, so these calls most likely happened before the 10:41 deactivation
Add a security group rule that denies 203.0.113.9, so that the attacker's address can no longer reach the account

explanation.correct: The 10:55 calls are signed with a different key, AKIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE, belonging to svc-metrics-ro, a user the exposed key created at 10:02 and gave AdministratorAccess (ATT&CK T1136.003 and T1098.001). Rotating the leaked key closed one door after the attacker had built another. Containment must cover everything the exposed key did: list its CloudTrail events since exposure (users, access keys, login profiles, roles, policies, compute) and disable or remove each, deactivating before deleting (the order AWS's compromise guidance uses for exposed keys), which keeps each change reversible and the objects available for investigation. The GetObject on example-customer-exports also means data access must be scoped for notification.

distractors.a: The old key's deactivation is not the issue: the 10:55 calls use a different access key ID that the attacker created.
distractors.c: CloudTrail delivery can lag, but each event records when the call was made; a timing artefact would not explain a brand-new key ID.
distractors.d: Security groups filter traffic to resources such as EC2 instances, not calls to AWS APIs; an IP block is also bypassed by changing address.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat a leaked cloud credential as a possible foothold factory and scope everything it created.

questions.question: At a software company, three users granted consent to a third-party app called 'PDF Signer Online' that requested mail read access and offline access. Logs show the app reading their mailboxes from 198.51.100.40. Which containment step removes the app's foothold in the tenant?

options.text: Reset the passwords of the three users who consented and consider the incident contained
Disable the app's service principal and remove its permission grants
Delete the enterprise application so that no trace of it remains in the tenant
Block 198.51.100.40 on the corporate perimeter firewall for all inbound and outbound traffic

explanation.correct: The attacker's access is the app's consent grant, not the users' passwords. Disabling the service principal stops Microsoft Entra ID from issuing new tokens to the app (an access token already issued runs until it expires), and removing its delegated permission grants and reviewing every user who consented closes the foothold. Microsoft's app-consent playbook recommends disabling rather than deleting, because a deleted app can return if another user consents again. Restricting user consent (for example to verified publishers and low-risk permissions) is the follow-up hardening.

distractors.a: The consent grant exists independently of the password; a reset does not remove the app's authorisation in the tenant.
distractors.c: Deleting looks thorough, but if another user consents again the app comes back; disabling keeps it blocked and preserves the object for investigation.
distractors.d: The app calls Microsoft's cloud APIs from the internet; that traffic never crosses the corporate firewall.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that in the cloud the foothold is often a grant or a token, not a machine or a password.

references.title: Microsoft incident response playbook: app consent grant investigation
MITRE ATT&CK T1528 Steal Application Access Token

questions.question: A compromised EC2 web server has a reverse shell open to 203.0.113.50. To contain it while keeping the instance running for memory capture, an engineer removed every inbound and outbound rule from its security group, but the shell session stays alive. What explains this, and what cuts it?

options.text: Security group changes can take up to a day to propagate; wait and confirm that the session drops
Security groups do not cut connections they already track; a network ACL deny for 203.0.113.50 does
Security groups filter only inbound traffic, so an outbound shell is never affected; stop the instance instead
The shell must be running over IPv6, which security groups cannot filter; disable IPv6 on the VPC

explanation.correct: AWS documents that when you change a security group rule, its tracked connections are not immediately interrupted; packets keep flowing until the existing connection times out. Network ACLs are stateless, so a deny rule (numbered ahead of the allow rules, because rules are evaluated from the lowest number) breaks the existing connection. A network ACL applies to the whole subnet, so scope the deny to the attacker's address to limit collateral, and snapshot the EBS volumes for disk evidence before any rebuild.

distractors.a: Rule changes apply quickly; the symptom comes from connection tracking, not propagation delay.
distractors.c: Security groups have outbound rules too, and stopping the instance destroys the memory you wanted to capture.
distractors.d: Security groups filter IPv6 as well as IPv4, and nothing here points to IPv6; documented connection tracking explains the symptom.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know cloud network controls have their own semantics, such as stateful tracking, that can defeat a quick isolation.

references.title: Amazon EC2 security group connection tracking
Amazon VPC: control subnet traffic with network access control lists

questions.subtopic: data-leakage containment: insider or compromised account
questions.question: At 23:00 a bank's monitoring shows a contractor's account bulk-downloading files from a SharePoint site of client due-diligence documents: 2,000 files in 40 minutes from an unmanaged device, still running. You cannot yet tell whether the contractor is acting or the account is compromised. What is the right containment decision?

options.text: Keep watching until the morning, when the contractor's manager can confirm whether the activity is expected
Turn off external sharing for the whole tenant tonight so that nothing more can leave the bank
Phone the contractor to ask what they are doing before taking any action on the account
Block the account's sign-in, revoke its sessions and preserve the audit records

explanation.correct: Whether insider or account takeover, the access path is the same identity, so the same containment applies and you do not need to settle the question first. Blocking sign-in and revoking sessions stops new downloads; Microsoft lists compromised accounts, termination and insider threats among the reasons for this emergency revocation. Preserve the evidence early: search both FileDownloaded (browser) and FileSyncDownloadedFull (sync client), because a search on one alone can miss part of the volume, and export the records rather than relying on audit retention. Contact with the contractor, their employer and any legal step is for HR, legal and vendor management.

distractors.a: Client data keeps leaving for hours while you wait; the activity is already abnormal enough to contain and explain later.
distractors.b: The files are being downloaded by a signed-in account, not shared externally, so a tenant-wide sharing change misses the channel and disrupts everyone.
distractors.c: If the contractor is acting, the call tips them off; if the account is compromised, it wastes time while the download continues.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you contain on the access path without first having to prove intent.

questions.subtopic: ransomware containment: source host vs account vs victim server
questions.question: At 03:10 a client's file server FS01 shows files being renamed and encrypted over SMB. The open-sessions list on FS01 shows the writes come from workstation WS-118 (EDR installed) using the account a.popescu. Which single action stops the encryption fastest while preserving evidence?

options.text: Network-isolate WS-118 through the EDR agent
Shut down FS01 to protect the files still unencrypted
Disable a.popescu in Active Directory
Block the ransomware family's known C2 domain at the proxy

explanation.correct: The encrypting process runs on WS-118 and reaches FS01 over SMB, so isolating WS-118 cuts every SMB session it holds, to FS01 and any other share, in one action while keeping its memory (which may hold the encryptor and its configuration) for forensics. CISA's ransomware guide describes this check: when server-side data is being encrypted by an infected workstation, use the server's sessions and open files to find the source. Next, disable and reset a.popescu, sweep for the same binary elsewhere and check where else the account was used.

distractors.b: Shutting down FS01 stops writes to that server only, takes the file service down for everyone and leaves WS-118 free to attack other shares.
distractors.c: Disabling the account blocks new authentications, but an SMB session that is already established can keep working, and the process on WS-118 keeps running.
distractors.d: Encryption over SMB does not need an outbound C2 connection; blocking the domain does not stop writes already in progress.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you contain at the source of the activity rather than at the victim or at the identity alone.

references.title: CISA #StopRansomware Guide (containment and eradication)
MITRE ATT&CK T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

questions.subtopic: cloud-era containment with no machine to isolate
questions.question: At a SaaS vendor, a support engineer's session to the internal admin console was hijacked with a session cookie stolen from the engineer's personal, unmanaged laptop. Over two hours the attacker viewed customer API secrets and created two external sharing links on a support folder. Which THREE actions contain this? (Choose 3.)

options.text: Revoke the engineer's sessions in the identity provider and end their sessions in the admin console
Rotate the customer API secrets that were viewed, coordinating the change with the affected customers
Wait until the engineer brings the laptop in for imaging before taking any action on the account
Remove the two external sharing links and review the access logs for any use of them
Reset the engineer's password, which on its own invalidates every session and cookie the attacker holds

explanation.correct: There is no company machine to isolate, so containment happens on the identity, the secrets and the sharing. Revoking sessions at the identity provider stops new tokens, but an application's own session cookie is controlled by that application (Microsoft notes that Entra ID cannot directly revoke a session token issued by an app), so the session must also be ended in the console. Secrets that were viewed must be treated as exposed and rotated, and the links removed and checked for use. The laptop can be examined later to learn how the cookie was stolen.

distractors.c: The laptop is unmanaged and may never be handed over; waiting leaves the hijacked session, the viewed secrets and the open links in place.
distractors.e: A password reset does not end an application's own session cookie, and the stolen cookie already carries a completed sign-in; sessions must be revoked explicitly.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can contain a cloud incident when there is no host to isolate.

questions.subtopic: long-term containment for a system that cannot stop
questions.question: A compromised server runs a bank's end-of-day settlement batch and cannot be taken down until the weekend rebuild window, five days away. The attacker's C2 is blocked, their backdoor account is disabled, memory and disk evidence are collected, and no activity has been seen for 24 hours. What is appropriate containment until the rebuild?

options.text: Leave the server as it is, because with the C2 blocked and the backdoor account disabled the incident is already contained
Rebuild it in place tonight during the batch window without testing, so that the risk is removed as soon as possible
Restrict its flows and admin access, rotate its credentials, monitor closely and have the system owner accept the residual risk
Shut it down now and run the settlement manually for five days, whatever the operational cost turns out to be

explanation.correct: Long-term containment is a temporary state that lets a system keep doing its job while a clean replacement is prepared. Because you cannot prove the attacker has no other foothold on the server, you shrink what any remaining foothold can reach (only required flows, administration through a monitored jump host, rotated credentials), raise detection on it, and make the residual risk an explicit, time-bound decision by the system owner. NIST SP 800-61r2 lists service availability and the duration of the solution among the criteria for choosing a containment strategy.

distractors.a: Blocking one C2 and one account removes only the known access; an attacker who had the server may have other channels, so it needs reduced exposure and closer watch.
distractors.b: An untested rebuild of a settlement system risks failed or wrong settlement, a bigger incident than the controlled risk you are managing.
distractors.d: Defensible only if the risk were extreme; with no activity for 24 hours and compensating controls available, five days of manual settlement is disproportionate and error-prone.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can keep a critical system running safely and make residual risk someone's explicit decision.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (section 3.3.1)

questions.question: A bank's DLP alert shows that a treasury analyst who handed in her notice last week uploaded one spreadsheet of client data to a personal cloud storage site yesterday. Before the incident manager estimates impact, how should you scope the leak?

options.text: Investigate the alerted upload only, since it is the one event the DLP policy matched
Review all of the user's outbound channels over a look-back window that starts before the notice
Ask the employee to list everything they took and use that list as the scope
Limit the scope to the clients in the uploaded spreadsheet and start notifying them today so the bank is not late

explanation.correct: One alert is a sample, not the scope. Departing-employee cases often involve collection over weeks and across channels (email, web upload, removable media, print, sync clients), and a DLP policy only matches what its conditions cover: renamed, compressed or unlabelled files can pass without a match. Scope by account, devices and channels over a look-back window that starts before the notice was given, since intent often predates the notice, within what your logs still hold (Microsoft 365 Audit Standard keeps records for 180 days). Only then estimate which data and clients are affected.

distractors.a: Investigating only what matched assumes the policy saw everything; unmatched files and other channels would be missed and impact underestimated.
distractors.c: The subject's own account is unreliable and alerts them early; interviews come later, planned with HR and Legal, after the logged evidence is secured.
distractors.d: Notification follows a scoped assessment; deciding from one file risks both missing affected clients and sending inaccurate notices.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat a single alert as the start of an investigation rather than its boundary.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: During an intrusion at a bank, EDR shows the attacker compressed a folder of customer exports into a password-protected archive, and the proxy shows a 640 MB upload from the same host to an external IP minutes later. Management asks how many customers are affected. What is the soundest basis for the estimate?

options.text: Divide the 640 MB uploaded by the average size of one customer record in the core banking export format
Report zero affected customers, because the archive was encrypted and the attacker cannot be shown to have opened it
The files that went into the archive, established from the command line, file-access events and the source folder
Wait until the data appears on a leak site and count the records published there

explanation.correct: Bytes on the wire do not convert to records: the archive is compressed and encrypted, protocols add overhead, and one upload may be only part of the transfer. The defensible estimate comes from the content: the archiving command line and file-access telemetry show which files were read, and the source folder (or a recovered copy of the staged archive) shows how many customers those files hold. The 640 MB then works as a cross-check: if the selected files would compress to much more, look for other uploads or channels. Until the content is confirmed, report a range and state the assumptions.

distractors.a: Compression ratios differ widely between file types, so a bytes-per-record division can be wrong by an order of magnitude in either direction.
distractors.b: The attacker's password protects nothing for the bank, since the attacker holds it. Encryption lowers risk only when it is the bank's own protection that keeps the data unintelligible to the attacker.
distractors.d: Publication may never happen or may be partial, and the impact assessment and any regulatory clock cannot wait for the attacker.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can turn raw telemetry into a defensible impact statement instead of a guess.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
MITRE ATT&CK T1560.001: Archive via Utility

questions.question: At a client, your working hypothesis is that the attacker entered through the VPN with a phished password, because the user clicked a phishing link two days before the first malicious activity. How should you test this hypothesis?

options.text: Check the logs for what must exist if it is true, such as a VPN session for that account from unfamiliar infrastructure
Gather more evidence of the phishing itself (the email, the click, the landing page) until the case looks convincing to the client
Present it to the client as the root cause, since the timing fits and the report is due
Reset the user's password and treat the hypothesis as confirmed if the malicious activity stops afterwards

explanation.correct: A hypothesis is tested through its predictions, including the ones that could disprove it. If the VPN theory holds, there must be a VPN session for that account from infrastructure the user does not normally use, shortly before the first malicious activity, and traffic from the VPN address pool to the first compromised host. If the logs show no such session, the theory fails even though the phishing click is real, and other entry vectors (an exposed service, another account) stay open. Write down what would refute each hypothesis before looking at the data.

distractors.b: This proves the click, which nobody disputes; it never tests the link from click to intrusion. Collecting only agreeing evidence is confirmation bias.
distractors.c: Timing alone is correlation. An untested root cause becomes the client's remediation plan, and a wrong one leaves the real entry point open.
distractors.d: Containment changes the environment and is not a test: activity can stop because the attacker pauses or switches accounts, so the result proves nothing either way.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you look for evidence that could prove you wrong, not only evidence that agrees.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
MITRE ATT&CK T1133: External Remote Services

questions.question: During a bank intrusion, the C2 IP address appears in a threat-intelligence feed linked to a named state-sponsored group, and the malware contains comments in a foreign language. The CISO wants to tell the board and the regulator who is behind the attack. What should the IR lead advise?

options.text: Name the group: a feed match on infrastructure together with language artefacts is enough for attribution
Report the actor as unknown and leave the feed match out of all reports to avoid any speculation
Name the group and scope the incident from its published playbook, since that shows which systems it usually targets
Report an overlap with the group's reported indicators, with a confidence level, and keep the response evidence-led

explanation.correct: Infrastructure and language artefacts are weak attribution evidence on their own: IP addresses are rented, shared and reused, tools are sold or leaked, and strings can be planted as false flags. MITRE ATT&CK itself notes that organisations' group definitions overlap and may disagree on specific activity. The sound message states the overlap, the evidence behind it and a confidence level. Containment, scoping and notification rest on what happened in the bank's environment, which does not depend on the actor's name.

distractors.a: A feed match and language strings show overlap, not identity; naming an actor to the board and the regulator on that basis can be wrong and hard to retract.
distractors.b: Hiding a relevant intelligence lead is the opposite error; the overlap is useful context when its confidence is stated.
distractors.c: Published TTPs can suggest where to look, but scope must come from your own evidence; attackers vary, and here the attribution itself is uncertain.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you separate useful threat-intel context from unsupported attribution claims under executive pressure.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Groups
NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: In an insider case at a bank, endpoint telemetry shows client files copied to drive E: on a workstation. HR will ask the employee to hand over the device used. Which recorded detail best identifies that specific USB device?

options.text: The drive letter E: that Windows assigned when the device was connected to the workstation
The volume label of the drive as shown in the file manager
The vendor ID, product ID and serial number in the device-connection record
The hashes of the copied files, which will match the files on the device

explanation.correct: Windows assigns drive letters dynamically and users can rename volume labels, so neither identifies hardware. The device-connection record (EDR or DLP device events, or the Windows device-installation artefacts) holds the vendor ID, product ID and serial number, which can be matched to the device handed over. Caveat: some cheap devices report no unique serial, in which case Windows generates an instance ID instead, so record exactly what the artefact shows. File hashes become useful later, to prove which files are on the device once you have it.

distractors.a: Drive letters are reused: the next stick plugged in may also become E:, so the letter cannot single out one device.
distractors.b: A volume label is user-editable and often left at the manufacturer default, so many devices share it.
distractors.d: Hashes confirm content once you hold the device, but they cannot tell you which device to ask for, and files may have been deleted from it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know which artefacts identify hardware rather than a moment of use.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001: Exfiltration over USB

questions.question: A bank's SOC tells the risk committee that mean time to respond fell from 9 hours to 3 hours this quarter. In the same quarter, an automation playbook started auto-closing duplicate phishing reports within minutes, and those closures count as incidents. What should the committee be told about this figure?

options.text: The near-zero auto-closures drag the average down, so real incidents may be handled no faster than before
The figure is accurate and can go to the committee as it is, because the automation genuinely made the SOC faster
The figure also shows that detection coverage improved, because many more incidents were closed
Time to respond is unreliable and should be replaced by the count of incidents closed per quarter

explanation.correct: An average over a changed population is not comparable across quarters. Hundreds of auto-closed items with near-zero durations pull the mean down even if every real incident took exactly as long as before. Report auto-closures separately and show real incidents by severity or type, including the longest ones: incident durations are heavily skewed, so a single average (mean or median) says little on its own. State where the clock starts and stops, so the committee compares like with like.

distractors.b: Some gain is real for analyst workload, but the committee will read the number as faster handling of incidents, which the data no longer shows.
distractors.c: Closing duplicates faster says nothing about how many real attacks are detected; time to respond measures speed on incidents already found.
distractors.d: A closure count rewards volume, not speed or quality, and is even easier to inflate with automation.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can explain to non-technical leaders why a metric moved, not just report it.

references.title: Google SRE: Incident Metrics in SRE

questions.question: Your timeline shows initial access on 3 March and lateral movement on 9 March, with nothing in between. You then learn that the domain controllers' Security logs roll over after about four days at their current size, and the oldest DC event you hold is an ordinary logon from 8 March. How should the 3-8 March period be described in the report?

options.text: As a dormant period in which the attacker did nothing between initial access and lateral movement
As a sign that the 3 March initial access is probably wrong, since no follow-up activity was logged after it
As a visibility gap for DC activity, with its cause stated, pending checks of other sources
As anti-forensics: the attacker cleared the DC logs to hide what happened between the two dates

explanation.correct: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence when the source did not exist for the period. Size-based rollover overwrote the DC Security events before 8 March, so the report should call 3-8 March a visibility gap for DC activity, state why, and list the other places to check: events already forwarded to the SIEM, EDR telemetry, logs on member servers, log backups. The improvement action is to size or forward DC logs so they cover a realistic investigation window.

distractors.a: Dormancy is a claim about attacker behaviour that the data cannot support; the logs that would show activity no longer exist.
distractors.b: The initial-access evidence comes from its own sources; missing later logs do not make an earlier logged event false.
distractors.d: Overwriting by size is normal log behaviour. Clearing the Security log records Event 1102; without that or other tampering evidence, anti-forensics is not shown.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you distinguish what the attacker did not do from what you cannot see.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management
NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: A software vendor's customer portal was compromised with a web shell. The team deleted the web shell, rotated credentials and closed the incident. Three weeks later a new web shell appears in the same upload directory. What did the first response most likely miss?

options.text: A full rebuild of the server, which on its own would have prevented the reinfection
How the web shell got onto the server, so the entry point was never fixed
Attribution of the attacker, which would have shown whether they intended to come back
A stricter antivirus policy, because the new web shell must be a variant the scanner missed

explanation.correct: Deleting the web shell removed the artefact, not the cause. Root-cause analysis asks how it got there: web server logs around the file's creation time usually show the request that wrote it, pointing to a vulnerable upload function or an exposed credential. NIST SP 800-61r3 asks responders to find the underlying or systemic root causes, not just the symptoms. With the same directory and technique three weeks later, the original entry point was almost certainly still open.

distractors.a: A rebuild removes persistence the team might have missed, but a rebuilt server running the same vulnerable code is reinfected the same way.
distractors.c: Knowing who attacked does not close the entry point; the fix comes from the access path, not the actor.
distractors.d: Better detection may spot it sooner, but the real question is why an attacker could write a file there at all.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you distinguish removing an artefact from closing the way in.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1505.003: Web Shell
NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: Why do many incident teams run post-incident reviews in a blameless format?

options.text: To keep the timeline anonymous, so that it records no names, roles or individual actions at all
To close the review quickly when human error is clearly the cause
To remove the need for action items with named owners and deadlines
So people report candidly and the review finds the conditions that allowed the incident

explanation.correct: Blameless does not mean anonymous or without ownership: the timeline still records who did what and when, and actions still get owners and deadlines. What changes is the goal. If people fear blame they hide or soften details, and the review stops at 'operator error'. A blameless review asks why an action made sense at the time and which conditions (tooling, alerts, playbooks, staffing) allowed it, which produces fixes that prevent recurrence.

distractors.a: The review needs an accurate record of actions; blameless describes how findings are treated, not deleting facts.
distractors.b: Human error is where the analysis starts, not where it ends: the question is why the error was possible and not caught.
distractors.c: Corrective actions still need named owners and due dates, otherwise lessons are never implemented.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you see blameless reviews as a way to surface systemic causes, not to avoid accountability.

references.title: Google SRE book: Postmortem Culture, Learning from Failure
NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.subtopic: root cause and the regulatory final report
questions.question: A bank classified an ICT-related incident as major under DORA and has sent the initial notification and an intermediate report. Services are restored and mitigation is in place, but the root-cause analysis is still running. A manager proposes sending the final report now. What is the correct position?

options.text: Send it now, because the final report is due as soon as services are restored
Not yet: it follows a completed root-cause analysis and actual impact figures, whether or not mitigation is done
Wait until every corrective action from the review is implemented, because the final report must confirm all fixes
Send it now and add the root cause later in a voluntary update to the competent authority

explanation.correct: DORA art. 19(4)(c) calls for the final report when the root-cause analysis has been completed, regardless of whether mitigation measures have already been implemented, and when actual impact figures are available to replace estimates. Under delegated Regulation 2025/301 it is due within one month of the last intermediate report. Restored service is a recovery milestone, not the end of the analysis. Separately, art. 13(2) requires a post-incident review after a major ICT-related incident that disrupts core activities, so the same root-cause work also feeds internal improvement.

distractors.a: Restoration is not the trigger; a final report without the root cause would lack what the regulation expects it to contain.
distractors.c: The regulation explicitly does not wait for mitigation measures to be implemented; the trigger is the completed root-cause analysis and actual figures.
distractors.d: This inverts the sequence: the final report is the one meant to carry the root cause and the actual impact.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you connect root-cause analysis to the bank's regulatory reporting, not only to internal learning.

references.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), EUR-Lex

questions.question: A breach at a SaaS vendor was discovered when a customer reported their data for sale; no SOC alert had fired. In the post-incident review, which analysis gives detection engineering the most useful output?

options.text: Count how many existing rules map to ATT&CK techniques and raise coverage wherever the count is low
Add the attacker's IP addresses, domains and file hashes to the blocklists and SIEM watchlists
Raise the severity of all existing alerts so that analysts review more of them
Map each timeline step to ATT&CK: was there telemetry, was there a rule, and why did nothing fire?

explanation.correct: A gap analysis anchored on the real timeline shows exactly where you were blind: missing telemetry (onboard the source), telemetry without a rule (write one), or a rule that did not fire or was dismissed (tune it or fix triage). Prioritise the earliest steps where detection was feasible, because they shorten dwell time most. NIST SP 800-61r3 names this kind of improvement explicitly: identifying TTPs that are not currently blocked by safeguards or flagged by detection technologies.

distractors.a: A coverage count shows which techniques have some rule, not whether the rules would have caught this attacker's behaviour with your telemetry.
distractors.b: Indicators from one incident are cheap for the attacker to change (low on the Pyramid of Pain); useful short-term, but not a detection improvement.
distractors.c: Raising every severity adds noise and alert fatigue without closing any specific gap.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you turn an incident into specific, prioritised detection work rather than generic coverage numbers.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
David Bianco: The Pyramid of Pain

questions.question: Reviewing a client's account-compromise incident, you find the containment playbook said only 'reset the password', which the analyst did at 10:05. Sign-in and mailbox audit logs show the attacker's IP kept accessing the mailbox until 14:30 without a new interactive sign-in. Which playbook change addresses this finding?

options.text: Change the step to reset the password twice, as recommended for on-premises Active Directory
Add a step to isolate the user's laptop from the network through EDR
Add explicit session and token revocation, then verify in the logs that the access stopped
Lower the impossible-travel detection threshold so that the next compromise is caught earlier

explanation.correct: A password reset does not end every session. In Microsoft Entra ID, access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire (one hour by default), some refresh tokens and session cookies survive a password change, and session cookies issued by an application are controlled by that application. Microsoft's emergency-revocation guidance therefore combines disabling the account, resetting the password and revoking refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession). A containment step is complete only when verified: query sign-in and audit logs for activity from the attacker's infrastructure after the containment time, and check for persistence the attacker added, such as new MFA methods or inbox rules.

distractors.a: Resetting twice addresses pass-the-hash and replication delay in on-premises AD; it does nothing about sessions and tokens the attacker already holds in the cloud.
distractors.b: The attacker's session runs from their own infrastructure, not from the user's laptop, so isolating the laptop does not cut it.
distractors.d: Earlier detection is useful, but the finding is about containment that did not contain; a detection change leaves the playbook gap open.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you check that containment actually worked and fix the playbook step that failed.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Revoke user access in an emergency in Microsoft Entra ID
Microsoft Learn: Refresh tokens in the Microsoft identity platform (token revocation)

questions.question: A third party reports to your MSSP that the client's public IP 203.0.113.10 sent exploit attempts to their web server at 14:32:07 UTC. 203.0.113.10 is the client's outbound NAT address, shared by about 2,000 internal hosts. What do you need to identify the internal source?

options.text: The source port and exact timestamp from the reporter, matched against the client's NAT translation logs
The client's DHCP logs for 14:32, which map internal IP addresses to hosts
The client's firewall rule base, to see which internal subnets may use 203.0.113.10
The list of internal hosts with the most outbound traffic that day, since the attacker is likely the heaviest user

explanation.correct: With address sharing, the public IP matches thousands of sessions. The reporter's source port and an accurate timestamp (with time zone) narrow it to one entry in the NAT or firewall session log, which gives the internal IP and port. DHCP leases or EDR network telemetry then map that internal IP at that time to a host and user. RFC 6302 recommends that internet-facing servers log the source port and accurate timestamps for exactly this reason. Check the reporter's clock before matching.

distractors.b: DHCP maps internal IPs to hosts, but you do not yet have the internal IP; the NAT translation step comes first.
distractors.c: A rule base shows what is allowed, not which host made a given connection.
distractors.d: Traffic volume does not identify a connection; it picks a suspect instead of finding evidence.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can trace a connection through address translation, a step external abuse reports often make hard.

references.title: RFC 6302: Logging Recommendations for Internet-Facing Servers
NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: Why can the time to detect for an intrusion usually be calculated only after the investigation, not when the alert fires?

options.text: Because it runs from the alert to the analyst's first action, which happens later
Because its clock starts when the malicious activity began, which the timeline establishes
Because it runs from detection to containment, which is only known later
Because its clock stops at incident closure, which only comes at the very end of the investigation

explanation.correct: Time to detect runs from the start of malicious activity (for example the initial access) to detection. The alert gives the end point, but the start is unknown until the investigation reconstructs the sequence of events, and the first malicious event is often days or weeks before the first alert. That is also why the figure can grow as the investigation finds earlier activity. Definitions vary between organisations, so state where each clock starts and stops.

distractors.a: Alert to first analyst action is time to acknowledge or triage, a different metric that can be computed at once.
distractors.c: Detection to containment is time to contain; it starts where time to detect ends.
distractors.d: Closure belongs to time-to-resolve metrics; time to detect stops at detection.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know where each metric's clock starts and stops.

references.title: Google SRE: Incident Metrics in SRE
NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: While merging logs for a timeline, you notice that every connection the firewall records from one server appears in that server's own logs about 4 minutes 10 seconds earlier, consistently, including routine traffic. Both sources say they log in UTC. How should you handle this?

options.text: Treat the server's logs as tampered with, since their timestamps disagree with the firewall's
Drop the server's logs from the timeline and rely on the firewall only
Ignore the difference, since a few minutes cannot change the order of events in an incident
Measure and document the offset, then correct the server times while keeping the originals

explanation.correct: A constant offset across routine events is the signature of clock drift, not tampering. Measure it from anchor events visible in both sources, use a third NTP-synchronised source to tell which clock is wrong, and normalise in the timeline while preserving the original timestamps and noting the correction; then report the clock fault for fixing. NIST SP 800-92 notes that out-of-sync sources may need times added or subtracted, and that NTP should keep sources consistent. A four-minute error can reorder events that happen seconds apart, such as a logon and the process it starts.

distractors.a: Tampering would not shift every event, routine ones included, by the same amount; a consistent offset points to clock drift.
distractors.b: The server logs hold details the firewall lacks (processes, accounts); correcting the offset keeps that evidence usable.
distractors.c: Intrusion steps often happen seconds apart; a four-minute skew can put an effect before its cause.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can correlate sources whose clocks disagree without discarding or silently altering evidence.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: At a client, one workstation is confirmed to beacon over HTTPS to 198.51.100.23 from a malicious binary. Which THREE actions best establish the scope of the intrusion? (Choose three.)

options.text: Search proxy, firewall and DNS logs over the full retention period for other hosts that contacted 198.51.100.23 or its domain
Reimage the workstation now to stop the beacon, then watch for a week whether new alerts appear on other hosts
Search EDR telemetry across the estate for the binary's hash, name, path and persistence mechanism
Run an authenticated vulnerability scan of the whole network to find the other hosts the attacker compromised
Review authentications from the workstation and by the accounts used on it, to find systems reached next

explanation.correct: Scoping finds every asset and account the attacker touched, using what the first host reveals: its network indicators (other hosts talking to the same C2), its host indicators (the same binary or persistence elsewhere) and its credentials (where the accounts used on it were used next). NIST SP 800-61r3 recommends looking for indicators of compromise and persistence on both the known targets and other potential targets, because a superficial check underestimates the magnitude of an incident.

distractors.b: Reimaging first destroys the evidence that drives the pivots, and waiting for alerts relies on the same detections that missed this intrusion.
distractors.d: A vulnerability scan shows what could be exploited, not what was compromised; it finds no beacons, implants or misused accounts.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you pivot on network, host and identity indicators instead of treating the first host as the whole incident.

questions.question: True or false: after one host is confirmed compromised, a sweep of all EDR, proxy and DNS data for the incident's file hashes, IP addresses and domains finds no other hits. This shows that no other host is compromised.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. A negative sweep only shows that these exact indicators are absent from the data you searched. Attackers repack tools per host (new hashes), rotate infrastructure, and use valid accounts and built-in tools that leave no unique indicator. The sweep is also bounded by coverage (hosts without EDR, unmanaged devices) and by retention. Before declaring scope, search for behaviour: where the accounts from the compromised host were used, its lateral connections, and the persistence technique it used.

distractors.a: Equating 'no hits' with 'clean' ignores per-host indicators, living-off-the-land activity and gaps in telemetry coverage and retention.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know the limits of indicator-based scoping.

questions.question: A post-incident review at a software company records: a phishing email reached a developer; the developer entered credentials on a fake login page; the attacker signed in through a legacy protocol that the MFA policy did not cover; the sign-in alert fired but waited 14 hours in the queue because the night shift was unstaffed. Which TWO findings should the corrective action plan treat as root causes or contributing factors? (Choose two.)

options.text: The developer was careless and should be named in the report as the cause
Legacy authentication stayed enabled, so a stolen password worked without MFA
The attacker was skilled, so the incident could not reasonably have been prevented
The incident happened at night, outside normal business hours
Nobody covered the alert queue overnight, so a valid alert waited 14 hours

explanation.correct: Root causes and contributing factors are conditions the organisation controls whose fix would have prevented or limited the incident. Legacy authentication that bypassed MFA turned one phished password into access, and the unstaffed queue turned a working detection into a 14-hour delay. NIST SP 800-61r3 asks responders to find the underlying or systemic root causes. Someone clicking a convincing phish is expected now and then; the system should not let one click become a breach. Awareness training can still be an action, but blaming the user is not a root cause.

distractors.a: Naming a person as the cause stops the analysis at human error and discourages candid reporting; the systemic question is why one typed password was enough.
distractors.c: 'Skilled attacker' is not something the organisation can act on, and the facts show two controllable gaps.
distractors.d: The time of day is a circumstance; the condition you can fix is the missing overnight coverage, which is a separate finding.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you look past the human trigger to the controls that should have stopped it.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
Google SRE book: Postmortem Culture, Learning from Failure

questions.question: After an incident, you write a new detection for the technique the attacker used. Which THREE steps should be done before the lesson is considered closed? (Choose three.)

options.text: Run the rule over the incident's historical logs, or emulate the technique, to confirm it would have fired
Confirm that the query parses and runs without errors in the console, then enable it in production
Run it over recent production data to estimate alert volume and false positives, and tune it
Link the alert to a triage playbook that says what to check and what to do
Give it the highest severity so that it is never missed, and skip tuning to save time

explanation.correct: A detection only counts as a lesson learned if it demonstrably fires on the behaviour that hurt you, at a volume analysts can handle, and leads to the right action. Back-testing on the incident's data (or emulating the technique) proves it detects; running it over recent data shows whether noise will bury it; a linked playbook makes the alert actionable for L1. In Microsoft Sentinel, run the rule's KQL in Logs over the incident's time range before enabling it; in Splunk, run the SPL search over the same period.

distractors.b: A query that runs without errors can still match nothing (wrong table, field or value format); running is not validation.
distractors.e: Top severity without tuning floods the queue and teaches analysts to ignore it, the opposite of the goal.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat a detection as tested code rather than a one-off query.

questions.question: You are building the timeline of a compromised bank workstation. The EDR console shows local time (UTC+3); the email gateway and the proxy log in UTC. Put the events in the order they actually happened.

Email gateway, 08:02 UTC: message with invoice.docm delivered to the user
EDR, 11:52 local: 7z.exe creates q3_clients.7z in a temp folder
Proxy, 09:20 UTC: WS-0412 uploads 310 MB to 198.51.100.23

explanation.correct: Convert everything to UTC first: the EDR times become 08:14 and 08:52. The order is then delivery (08:02), the macro document starting PowerShell (08:14), the first C2 connection (08:16), staging the archive (08:52) and the upload (09:20). Sorting the raw clock values would put the C2 connection and the upload before the macro execution and the staging that caused them. Record each source's time zone and normalise to one zone before merging, as NIST SP 800-92 advises for log correlation.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you normalise time zones before ordering evidence from different tools.

questions.question: Put the steps of a post-incident review after a major ICT incident at a bank in order.

options.text: Track each action to closure and check that it had the intended effect
Agree corrective actions, each with an owner and a due date
Assemble the facts: final timeline, evidence, and decisions with their times
Present the review report, with findings and owned actions, to management
Analyse root causes and how well alerting, escalation and communication worked

explanation.correct: Analysis needs the facts first; actions follow from causes; management is told what was found and what will change; and the review closes only when actions are implemented and verified, since untracked actions are how the same lesson gets learned twice. For a bank, DORA art. 13(2) requires a post-incident review after a major ICT-related incident that disrupts core activities, assessing among other things how promptly security alerts were handled, the quality and speed of forensic analysis, escalation and internal and external communication; entities other than microenterprises must tell the competent authority, on request, what changes they made.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you see the review as ending with verified change, not with the meeting.

questions.question: Match each log source to the investigation question it answers best.

right.text: Which process, and which parent process, opened a network connection on a host
Which device held a given internal IP address at a given time
Which account signed in, from which IP, and whether MFA succeeded
Which software vulnerabilities a host currently has
Which URL was requested and how many bytes were sent and received

explanation.correct: Investigations chain sources: the proxy gives the URL, bytes and source IP; DHCP turns 'this IP at this time' into a device; EDR names the process behind the connection; the identity provider shows which account signed in, from where and with what MFA result. Vulnerability data (the extra item) describes exposure, not activity, and comes from a scanner rather than from any of these logs.

distractors.l2: A proxy sees the request, the source IP and often the user, but not which process on the host made it; that is EDR's view.
distractors.l1: DHCP knows nothing about accounts or MFA; it maps an IP address to a device (MAC address, hostname) over time.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know which source answers which question when building a case.
