questions.question: In a post-incident review for a client, match each finding to the corrective action that addresses it.

left.text: The compromised server had never sent its logs to the SIEM
A rule for the technique existed, but its threshold was so high that the attack stayed below it
The alert fired, but L1 closed it as benign because their guidance did not describe this pattern
Containment waited six hours for approval from a manager who could not be reached

right.text: Tune the rule with the incident data and back-test it
Define delegated authority and a backup approver in the escalation matrix
Onboard the source and alert when any source stops sending
Subscribe to an additional threat-intelligence feed
Update the triage playbook and brief L1 on the pattern

explanation.correct: Each finding points to a different layer: visibility (onboard the source and monitor for silence), detection logic (tune and back-test), triage (playbook and briefing) and decision rights (delegated authority). Mapping a finding to the layer that failed avoids generic fixes. An extra threat-intelligence feed addresses none of these gaps. NIST SP 800-61r3 counts both detection improvements and changes to plans, processes and procedures as outputs of lessons learned.

distractors.l3: Tuning is the wrong fix here: the rule fired correctly, and the failure was in the triage guidance.
distractors.l2: A playbook change cannot help while the alert never fires; the threshold itself has to change.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you turn review findings into the right kind of fix.

questions.question: Which proxy log line most warrants an exfiltration investigation?
questions.context:
#Fields: date time c-ip cs-username cs-method cs-host sc-status cs-bytes sc-bytes
2026-06-10 01:47:12 10.8.4.21 m.dobre GET updates.vendor.example 200 612 1873402911
2026-06-10 02:13:55 10.8.4.37 a.stan POST upload.filedrop.example 200 1288490188 1403
2026-06-10 02:14:02 10.8.4.37 a.stan GET cdn.news.example 200 845 524288
2026-06-10 02:20:31 10.8.4.52 v.ilie POST upload.filedrop.example 403 958 1210

options.text: Line 1, because it moves the most data in the log, about 1.8 GB
Line 2, because about 1.2 GB went from the client to a file-sharing host
Line 3, because it comes from the same user within seconds of line 2
Line 4, because a denied upload to a file-sharing site proves intent

explanation.correct: In W3C-style fields, cs-bytes counts client-to-server bytes (what the user sent) and sc-bytes server-to-client bytes (what the user received). Line 2 is a POST with about 1.2 GB in cs-bytes to a file-sharing host, accepted with status 200 at 02:13: data left the organisation. Line 1's 1.8 GB is in sc-bytes, a download from an update server. Next steps for line 2: identify the file (DLP or EDR file events), the device, and whether a.stan was really at the keyboard.

distractors.a: The large value is in sc-bytes, data received by the client, which fits an update download, not data leaving.
distractors.c: A small GET with a modest download is ordinary browsing; it only matters as context around line 2.
distractors.d: Status 403 with under 1 KB sent shows the proxy refused the request; worth a follow-up, but less urgent than a completed 1.2 GB upload, and one denial does not prove intent.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you read the direction of the bytes, not just the size.

2026-04-02 03:12:41  r.matei@corp.example               archive.box@mail.example   Payment confirmation 8841   Delivered

2026-04-02 10:31:41  r.matei@corp.example               archive.box@mail.example   Salary review 2026          Delivered

options.text: Automatic forwarding to an outside address; check the mailbox rules and forwarding, then who set them up
The user forwards mail by hand so they can keep working from home; remind them of the acceptable-use policy
An outside party is spoofing copies into the mailbox; block the sender domain mail.example
The user is replying to each sender as part of normal correspondence, so no action is needed

explanation.correct: Every inbound message, from any sender and even at 03:12, is followed one second later by a copy from r.matei to the same external address. That timing is machine behaviour, not a person. It fits an inbox rule or mailbox forwarding (ATT&CK T1114.003), set either by an attacker with access to the mailbox or by the user. Check the rules and forwarding configuration, then who created them and from which sign-in: in the Microsoft 365 audit log, New-InboxRule and Set-InboxRule record rules made in Outlook on the web, and UpdateInboxRules those made from the Outlook client. That answer decides between account compromise and an insider policy breach.

distractors.b: No one forwards by hand with a one-second delay on every message, including at 03:12.
distractors.c: The trace shows r.matei as the sender and the external address as the recipient; the problem is outbound copies, not inbound spoofing.
distractors.d: Replies would go back to each original sender; here every copy goes to the same external address within one second.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you read timing and direction in a trace to tell automation from a person.

questions.question: A bank's DLP team flags a mass download from a document-management site by employee d.pavel. Sign-in, audit and EDR records (UTC) are below. Which conclusion do they support?
questions.context:
Sign-ins
08:02  d.pavel  IP 10.12.3.44 (office)  device LAPTOP-DP01, managed, compliant  MFA satisfied  app: Office 365
13:41  d.pavel  IP 203.0.113.88  device not registered, Chrome on Windows  MFA passed (push approved)  app: SharePoint Online

SharePoint audit
13:45-14:20  d.pavel  FileDownloaded x612  site /sites/Retail-Credit  ClientIP 203.0.113.88
13:52        d.pavel  FileModified x1     site /sites/Team-DP        ClientIP 10.12.3.44

EDR
LAPTOP-DP01 on the office network with d.pavel logged on all afternoon

options.text: d.pavel downloaded the files on his corporate laptop, so an insider case should be opened against him
External account compromise is confirmed, so it should be reported to the regulator as an external attack
The files went to an unregistered outside device, not his laptop; who used it is not yet known
No data left the bank, because FileDownloaded only records files previewed in the browser

explanation.correct: Read the sessions, not just the username. All 612 FileDownloaded events (downloads through the browser) carry ClientIP 203.0.113.88, the session from an unregistered device, while the managed laptop was on the office network and editing a file at 13:52. So the files reached a device outside the bank's control. Two hypotheses fit: d.pavel used a personal device (for example on a mobile connection), or someone else had his password and got a push approved. Test them with the IP's history and owner, the details of the approved push and his registered devices, then plan any interview with HR. Until then: confirmed data movement to an unmanaged device, actor unconfirmed.

distractors.a: The laptop's activity came from the office IP; the downloads did not, so 'insider on the corporate laptop' contradicts the logs.
distractors.b: An approved push from an unknown IP does not prove an outside attacker; the employee on a personal device fits the same data, and a wrong report would have to be corrected.
distractors.d: FileDownloaded records a download through the browser; previews are logged as FilePreviewed. The data did reach the unregistered device.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you separate the account from the person and the device before naming an insider or an attacker.

questions.question: All times are normalised to UTC. What is the right reading of these records for bank employee c.rusu?

HQ-WS-1187 Security   07:58:40  EventID=4624  LogonType=2  TargetUserName=c.rusu
VPN gateway           08:06:03  user=c.rusu  src=203.0.113.77  geo=foreign country  result=success  MFA=OTP accepted
SRV-FILE03 Security   08:09:55  EventID=4624  LogonType=3  TargetUserName=c.rusu  IpAddress=10.250.0.18 (VPN pool)

options.text: c.rusu is travelling and a colleague used her badge, so the VPN alert can be closed as expected activity
She cannot easily be at her desk and abroad at once; investigate the VPN session as possible misuse
VPN geolocation is unreliable, so the foreign-country flag is a false positive and can be closed
Disable c.rusu's account and wipe HQ-WS-1187 at once, since the workstation is where the compromise started

explanation.correct: The badge-in at 07:51 and the interactive logon (LogonType 2) on HQ-WS-1187 at 07:58 place c.rusu, or someone with her badge and password, at her desk. Eight minutes later a VPN session for the same account succeeds from a foreign IP and makes a network logon (LogonType 3) to a file server from the VPN pool. The VPN session is the anomaly to test: an accepted OTP only shows the second factor was available to whoever connected, and OTPs can be phished. distractors.d: Nothing points to the workstation, whose session looks legitimate; wiping it destroys evidence, and containment should target the VPN session after quick validation.

attachment: chargebacks_q2.xlsx

host=SRV-DB02   2026-05-06T02:14:52Z  EventID=4624  LogonType=3  TargetUserName=svc_backup  IpAddress=10.20.4.37

questions.question: Your team follows the SANS PICERL model. An analyst reviews an EDR alert, confirms from the process tree and logon data that it reflects a real compromise rather than normal admin activity, and records which hosts are involved. Nothing has been isolated yet. Which phase is the analyst in?

options.text: Preparation
Identification
Containment
Lessons learned

explanation.correct: PICERL stands for Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons learned. Identification is where you decide whether a deviation from normal operations is an incident and gather what you need to scope it: validating the alert against the process tree and logon events and listing the affected hosts is exactly that. It corresponds to Detection & Analysis in the older NIST SP 800-61r2 cycle.

distractors.a: Preparation happens before any alert: policy, team, tooling, playbooks and training. Investigating a live alert is already past it.
distractors.c: Containment starts when you act to limit damage, for example isolating the host or disabling an account. The stem says nothing has been isolated yet.
distractors.d: Lessons learned is the last phase, after eradication and recovery: reviewing what happened and improving the process. The incident here has not even been contained.

explanation.interview_angle: Checks that you can place real analyst work in a named lifecycle instead of only reciting the acronym.

questions.question: A bank's information security incident procedure follows ISO/IEC 27035-1:2023. Put the five phases of its incident management process in order.

options.text: Respond: contain, eradicate and recover, collect evidence and communicate with stakeholders
Plan and prepare: incident management policy, response team, procedures, contacts and exercises
Learn lessons: review the handling and update controls, risk assessment and the incident management plan
Detect and report: staff, customers or monitoring tools spot and report information security events
Assess and decide: evaluate the reported events and decide whether they are an information security incident

explanation.correct: ISO/IEC 27035-1 describes five phases: Plan and prepare, Detect and report, Assess and decide, Respond, Learn lessons. The key distinction is between an information security event (something observed and reported) and an incident (an event, or series of events, assessed as able to harm the organisation's assets or operations). That decision is taken in Assess and decide, before the Respond phase commits people and money. In a bank it is also the natural point to start internal escalation and regulatory classification (for example whether an ICT incident is major under DORA). Learn lessons feeds improvements back into Plan and prepare.
explanation.interview_angle: Banks with an ISO 27001 ISMS expect you to know the 27035 vocabulary, especially the event versus incident decision.

references.title: ISO/IEC 27035-1:2023 Information security incident management - Part 1: Principles and process

questions.question: During an internal audit at a bank, the auditor flags the incident response procedure as non-compliant because it is built on SANS PICERL, and says NIST SP 800-61r3 requires its CSF 2.0-based model. How should the IR manager respond?

options.text: Agree, and rewrite the whole procedure around the six CSF 2.0 Functions before the next audit cycle so the bank is aligned with NIST
Point out that SP 800-61r3 was withdrawn and that the four-phase r2 cycle is again the NIST reference
Explain that r3 lets organisations use the life-cycle model that suits them, and show how each PICERL step maps to CSF outcomes
Keep PICERL but drop its Preparation phase, since r3 says preparation is not part of incident response

explanation.correct: SP 800-61r3 (April 2025) organises its recommendations as a CSF 2.0 Community Profile, but it states that organisations should use the incident response life-cycle framework or model that suits them best; what it insists on is that incident response is considered throughout cybersecurity risk management. A mapping from PICERL to CSF outcomes (Preparation to Govern, Identify and Protect; Identification to Detect; Containment, Eradication and Recovery to Respond and Recover; Lessons learned to the Improvement category of Identify) answers the audit point with evidence. For an EU bank, the binding requirements come from regulation such as DORA, not from NIST guidance.

distractors.a: A rewrite is not required: r3 explicitly leaves the choice of life-cycle model to the organisation, so a costly rewrite would not close any real gap.
distractors.b: Wrong direction: r3 supersedes r2 (the Computer Security Incident Handling Guide), not the reverse.
distractors.d: r3 says Govern, Identify and Protect are broader risk-management activities that support incident response, not that they are unnecessary. Dropping preparation removes the plan, roles and tooling the response depends on.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you know what changed in r3 and can defend a framework choice to an auditor without dogma.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: NIST SP 800-61r3 maps the phases of the previous SP 800-61r2 life cycle to CSF 2.0 Functions. Match each r2 phase to the Function(s) it mainly corresponds to.

right.text: Respond and Recover
Identify, Improvement category (ID.IM)
Govern, Identify and Protect
Detect
Protect only

explanation.correct: Table 1 of r3 maps Preparation to Govern, Identify (all categories) and Protect; Detection & Analysis to Detect; Containment, Eradication & Recovery to Respond and Recover; and Post-Incident Activity to the Improvement category (ID.IM) of Identify. r3 also lists ID.IM next to Detection & Analysis and next to Containment, Eradication & Recovery, because lessons can be learned at any point, not only at the end. In the r3 model, Govern, Identify and Protect are the preparation layer, Detect, Respond and Recover are incident response itself, and ID.IM is the continuous-improvement layer that feeds all of them.

distractors.l1: Pairing Preparation with Protect only is the common trap: r3 also puts governance (policy, roles, legal requirements) and asset and risk knowledge (Identify) into preparation.
distractors.l4: There is no separate lessons-learned Function in CSF 2.0; post-incident improvement lives in Identify as ID.IM.

explanation.interview_angle: Shows you can translate between the classic four-phase vocabulary most playbooks still use and the CSF-based r3 model.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
NIST CSWP 29 - The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0

questions.question: True or false: under NIST SP 800-61r3, lessons learned from an incident should be held back until recovery has finished, so that improvements are based on the complete picture.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. r3 explains that the old circular model, where post-incident activity fed preparation at the end, no longer fits incidents that last weeks or months, and that lessons learned should often be shared as soon as they are identified rather than after recovery concludes. In r3 every Function feeds the Improvement category (ID.IM), so a detection gap found on day 2 (for example a technique the EDR did not flag) should reach the detection engineers on day 2. r3 still describes a lessons-learned meeting as recovery concludes as a useful source of improvements, especially after a major incident (ID.IM-03), but it is not the only moment.

distractors.a: This was the logic of the r2 cycle, where Post-Incident Activity came last. r3 moved away from it because waiting lets the same gap be exploited again during a long incident.

explanation.interview_angle: Separates candidates who memorised the 2012 four-phase cycle from those who know how current guidance treats continuous improvement.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: A junior analyst opens an 'incident' for every alert in the queue, including 40 failed VPN logins from one external IP with no successful logon. Which statement correctly describes when an incident should be declared?

options.text: For every alert, because each detection rule in the SIEM was written to find attacks
Only once data loss has been confirmed; until then everything is an event
Only when the case must be reported to a regulator or other authority
When analysed adverse events meet the organisation's defined incident criteria

explanation.correct: In NIST SP 800-61r3 an event is any observable occurrence, an adverse event is one with a negative consequence, and an incident is an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardises confidentiality, integrity or availability, or violates (or imminently threatens to violate) law or security policy. CSF subcategory DE.AE-08 says incidents are declared when adverse events meet the defined incident criteria, taking known false positives into account. The 40 failed VPN logins are an adverse event to analyse (source reputation, targeted accounts, any later Event ID 4624 success); they become an incident only if they meet the criteria, for example a successful logon or a spray hitting many accounts.

distractors.a: Alerts are candidates, not verdicts: many are false positives or benign. Declaring each one an incident floods the IR process and hides the real ones.
distractors.b: Too narrow: the definition includes imminent threats, so an attacker with a working foothold is an incident before any data leaves.
distractors.c: Reporting duties (GDPR, DORA, NIS2) apply to some incidents after classification; they do not define what an incident is.

explanation.interview_angle: Basic but frequent: interviewers want to hear event, adverse event, incident and the idea of declared criteria.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: A client calls the MSSP hotline: their public website shows a defacement message. The MSSP monitors the client's web servers and WAF. What does the L1 analyst do first?

options.text: Confirm the report from the data you monitor (page, web and WAF logs), then estimate severity and urgency
Tell the client to shut down all of their internet-facing servers at once, until the cause of the change is known
Fill in the incident category, root cause and lessons-learned fields of the ticket before starting any analysis
Pass it to the client's web team as a content problem, since a defacement is not a security incident

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 (RS.MA-02, incident reports are triaged and validated) recommends a preliminary review to verify that an incident has occurred, then an estimate of its severity and the urgency of the response. Here that means checking the page and the web server and WAF logs you already collect (modified files, unusual POST requests or admin logons around the time of the change) and then assigning priority under the client's SLA. Detailed categorisation (RS.MA-03) and containment decisions follow once the facts are confirmed.

distractors.b: Over-containment before validation: shutting every internet-facing server can do more business damage than the defacement, and it is the client's decision, not the L1 analyst's.
distractors.c: Root cause and lessons learned cannot be written before the facts exist; detailed categorisation comes after validation.
distractors.d: Unauthorised modification of a website is an integrity incident and often a sign of a web shell or stolen admin credentials.

explanation.interview_angle: MSSP interviewers check that you validate, then prioritise, and do not improvise containment on a client's estate.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
MITRE ATT&CK T1491.002 - Defacement: External Defacement

questions.question: A user at an MSSP client reports a suspicious email containing a link. Put the L1 analyst's scoping steps in order.

options.text: For each recipient found, check proxy/DNS and sign-in logs after the delivery time for clicks or credential use
Escalate the users with clicks or suspicious sign-ins to L2, attaching the recipient list and indicators to the ticket
Validate the reported message (headers, sender domain, URL reputation) and extract its indicators
Search the mail logs with those indicators to list every recipient of the same campaign

explanation.correct: Each step needs the output of the previous one. First confirm the message is malicious and extract its indicators (sender address, subject, URL and domain, attachment hash). Those indicators drive the mail-log or message-trace search that lists every recipient, not only the person who reported it. Only with that list can you check who clicked or signed in afterwards (proxy or DNS logs, identity-provider sign-ins from new IPs). The escalation then carries what L2 needs: affected users, indicators and times. Microsoft's phishing playbook follows the same logic: review the email, find who else got it, then check whether users opened it or selected the link.
explanation.interview_angle: Checks that you scope a phishing report beyond the single reporter, in a logical order.

MITRE ATT&CK T1566.002 - Phishing: Spearphishing Link

questions.question: You have 15 minutes before shift handover and four unassigned alerts from different clients. Which alert do you work first?
questions.context:
SOC queue 02:10 UTC, handover 02:25, all alerts unassigned
A-17 | Client-1 | Brute force: 300 failed logons (Event ID 4625) | TEST-VM-07 (low) | 0 successful logons; source 203.0.113.40 blocked at firewall 01:55
A-18 | Client-3 | Malware quarantined | LAPTOP-HR-22 (standard) | adware; quarantine succeeded; no further activity in 2 h
A-19 | Client-2 | LSASS memory access | DC01 (domain controller) | rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 624 C:\Windows\Temp\d.dmp full; account svc-backup
A-20 | Client-4 | User-reported phishing | mailbox j.doe (standard) | message already removed from all mailboxes by the mail filter; no clicks logged

options.text: A-17, because it has by far the highest event count and arrived first in the queue
A-18, because it is the only alert where malware has been confirmed on a device
A-19, credential dumping on a domain controller
A-20, because a report from a human is more reliable than an automated rule

explanation.correct: A-19 is the only alert showing post-compromise activity on a critical asset: rundll32.exe calling comsvcs.dll MiniDump against a process ID (here 624, probably lsass.exe) is a known way to dump LSASS memory (T1003.001). On a domain controller, stolen credentials can mean domain-wide compromise, so asset criticality, stage of activity and potential impact all point the same way. Confirm the PID is lsass.exe and why svc-backup ran it, then escalate to the client's IR contact before handover. NIST SP 800-61r3 is explicit that incidents should not be handled first come, first served. Example hunt in Microsoft Defender XDR: DeviceProcessEvents | where ProcessCommandLine has "comsvcs.dll" and ProcessCommandLine has "MiniDump".

distractors.a: Volume and arrival order are not severity. The brute force produced no successful logon (no matching 4624), hit a low-value test VM, and the source is already blocked.
distractors.b: Confirmed, but already contained: the quarantine succeeded and nothing followed. It needs closure notes, not your last 15 minutes.
distractors.d: User reports are valuable, but this one is already remediated (message purged, no clicks). The reliability of the source does not outrank an active threat on a domain controller.

explanation.interview_angle: A classic shift-handover question: interviewers want prioritisation by asset criticality and attack stage, said out loud.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1003.001 - OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: A bank's SOC reviews these events for a payments operations employee. What do they most likely show, and what is the right next step?
questions.context:
Identity provider and mailbox audit, user a.ionescu@bank.example (payments operations)
2026-10-12 08:02:11Z signin  ip=198.51.100.23 (bank egress)  geo=RO  result=success  auth=password + push MFA  app=webmail  ua=Edge/Windows
2026-10-12 08:41:57Z signin  ip=203.0.113.77 (hosting provider)  geo=NL  result=success  auth=existing session token, MFA claim reused  app=webmail  ua=python-requests
2026-10-12 08:43:20Z mailbox  op=new-inbox-rule  name="."  if subject or body contains "payment" or "IBAN" -> move to "RSS Feeds", mark as read  client_ip=203.0.113.77
2026-10-12 08:44:05Z mailbox  op=mail-items-read  count=212  client_ip=203.0.113.77

options.text: A business trip to the Netherlands: both sign-ins passed MFA, so the second one is the user; close the alert as benign travel
Token theft setting up payment fraud: treat as a compromise, pivot on 203.0.113.77 and the rule in all mailboxes
A successful password spray: a password reset ends the attacker's access, so reset it and close the ticket
The user reorganising their own mailbox with a filter rule: low severity, refer it to HR for a policy reminder

explanation.correct: The second sign-in reused an existing session token (no fresh password or MFA prompt) from a hosting-provider IP in another country 40 minutes after a normal sign-in, with a scripted user agent. That fits a stolen web session cookie or token being replayed (T1539, T1550.004), for example after adversary-in-the-middle phishing or infostealer malware on the endpoint. Two minutes later the same IP creates a rule that hides mail about payments or IBANs (T1564.008) and reads 212 messages: classic preparation for payment-redirection fraud against the bank's customers or counterparties. Scope before you close anything: all sign-ins from 203.0.113.77 and its network, the same rule pattern in other mailboxes, how the token was stolen, and which customers or payments appear in the messages read, because that drives customer contact and any regulatory assessment. Microsoft Sentinel examples: SigninLogs | where IPAddress == "203.0.113.77" and OfficeActivity | where Operation in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule").

distractors.a: MFA was satisfied by a reused token, not by the user approving a prompt; a stolen token works from anywhere until it is revoked. The country jump, hosting IP and python user agent all contradict travel.
distractors.c: There are no failed attempts, so nothing suggests spraying, and a password reset alone does not invalidate a token that has already been issued: active sessions must be revoked as well.
distractors.d: A rule named '.' that hides payment and IBAN mail, created from a foreign hosting IP, is a known attacker technique, not housekeeping. Treating it as HR misconduct leaves the attacker in the mailbox.

explanation.interview_angle: Bank interviewers use this to see whether you know that MFA success is not proof of legitimacy and that fraud scoping starts from attacker infrastructure.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.004 - Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
MITRE ATT&CK T1564.008 - Hide Artifacts: Email Hiding Rules

questions.question: A software company's IR lead reviews these EDR results. Which two conclusions are supported? (Choose 2)
questions.context:
EDR process events, pivot on SHA256 9f2c...e41, 2026-10-03 (UTC)
Time      Host        File         SHA256      Parent process
09:12:44  WS-DEV-114  updater.exe  9f2c...e41  winword.exe (document opened from an Outlook attachment)
11:40:02  WS-DEV-087  updater.exe  9f2c...e41  wmiprvse.exe
11:41:30  BUILD-02    updater.exe  9f2c...e41  wmiprvse.exe

Second search: parent = wmiprvse.exe, 11:30-12:00, all hosts
11:43:10  WS-DEV-201  svc_upd.exe  71ab...0c3  wmiprvse.exe

options.text: WS-DEV-114 is the most likely first host, infected through a document attachment
svc_upd.exe on WS-DEV-201 has a different hash from the pivot file, so it is unrelated and can be left out of scope
Blocking SHA256 9f2c...e41 on every endpoint in the company will be enough to contain the incident and stop its spread
Later hosts were reached by WMI execution within minutes: pivot on that behaviour and the account used, not just the hash
BUILD-02 was infected first, because build servers download updates automatically

explanation.correct: The earliest execution (09:12) has winword.exe as parent after an Outlook attachment was opened, which fits spearphishing with an attachment (T1566.001) on WS-DEV-114. The later executions all have wmiprvse.exe, the WMI provider host, as parent and occur within about three minutes of each other, which fits remote execution through WMI (T1047) from an already compromised host. svc_upd.exe on WS-DEV-201 appears in the same window with the same parent: a different hash is exactly what you expect when an attacker recompiles or renames a tool, so it stays in scope until proven otherwise. Next pivots: the account that made the WMI calls (network logons, Event ID 4624 logon type 3, on the targets) and every other host it touched. Hashes sit at the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain because they are trivial for an attacker to change.

distractors.b: Excluding it on the hash alone is the classic scoping error. Same parent process, same time window and a similar name are stronger evidence than a hash mismatch.
distractors.c: A hash block stops only this exact file; WS-DEV-201 already shows a different binary, and the WMI access and the credentials used would still work.
distractors.e: The timestamps contradict it: BUILD-02 ran the file at 11:41, more than two hours after WS-DEV-114, and its parent is WMI, not an updater.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you scope on behaviour and parent-child relationships instead of trusting a single IOC.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1047 - Windows Management Instrumentation
David Bianco - The Pyramid of Pain

questions.question: A bank's SOC sees a service account querying an internal API for customer account balances at 40 times its normal volume. To set the initial severity, which three questions should triage answer first? (Choose 3)

options.text: Which customer data, and roughly how many customers, could be or have been exposed?
Which named threat group is behind it, so that the severity reflects the attacker's reputation?
Is the activity still going on, and how far has it progressed?
Which vendor's product raised the alert, so that the right support contract is used?
How critical are the API and the service it supports to the bank's operations and customers?

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 gives examples of risk factors for prioritising incidents: asset criticality, functional impact, data impact, stage of observed activity, threat-actor characterisation and recoverability. In the first hour the answerable and decisive ones are data impact (which customer data, how many records), stage (still active or not, has data left) and the criticality of the affected service. The same facts feed the bank's later decisions: the GDPR assessment if personal data is involved, DORA classification (clients affected, data losses, critical services) and the first update to management. Record what is unknown as well as what is known.

distractors.b: Threat-actor characterisation helps later, but attribution is rarely available in the first hour and severity must not wait for it. A service account pulling customer balances is serious whoever is behind it.
distractors.d: The alert source matters for tuning and vendor support, not for how serious the incident is for the bank and its customers.

explanation.interview_angle: Bank interviewers want severity reasoning in terms of customers, data and critical services, not tool names or attribution.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: Which three elements belong in an incident response policy, as opposed to playbooks or technical procedures? (Choose 3)

options.text: The exact console steps for isolating a host in the EDR tool
Roles, responsibilities and authorities, such as who may disconnect or shut down systems
Definitions of events, incidents and related terms
The current list of malicious IP addresses, domains and file hashes that the SOC should block
Guidelines for prioritising incidents and estimating their severity

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 (section 2.3) lists the usual elements of an incident response policy: a statement of management commitment, purpose and objectives, scope, definitions of events, incidents and related terms, roles, responsibilities and authorities (for example which roles may confiscate, disconnect or shut down assets), guidelines for prioritisation, severity and recovery, and performance measures. Policies change rarely and are approved by management. Procedures and playbooks, based on the policy and plan, hold the actionable steps.

distractors.a: Tool-specific steps change with every product update; they belong in a procedure or playbook that the team maintains.
distractors.d: Indicators change daily and live in the SIEM, EDR or threat-intelligence platform, not in a management-approved policy.

explanation.interview_angle: Checks that you understand the document hierarchy: policy, plan, procedure, playbook.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: A SaaS company wants to be ready to investigate incidents in its cloud production accounts. Which three items should engineering verify before any incident happens? (Choose 3)

options.text: Control-plane and identity logs go to a central store, with retention that covers realistic attacker dwell times
Responders have pre-approved, tested access (dedicated IR roles or break-glass accounts) to the accounts and log stores
Verbose logging is planned to be switched on once an incident is declared, to save cost until then
Clocks on all log sources are synchronised and events are normalised to one time zone, such as UTC
The cloud provider keeps all customer activity logs indefinitely by default, so no retention planning is needed at all

explanation.correct: Investigation depends on data and access that must exist before the incident. NIST SP 800-61r3 stresses that log records are generated and available for monitoring (PR.PS-04) and collected centrally for correlation (DE.AE-03), and that people with response duties are given the authority they need in advance (GV.RR-02). Consistent clocks are what make cross-source timelines possible; SP 800-61r2 already recommended keeping host clocks synchronised for this reason. Testing access before an incident avoids losing hours to access requests, or to permissions an attacker has already changed.

distractors.c: Logging cannot be turned on retroactively: the actions before the declaration, often the most important ones (initial access, privilege changes), would be missing.
distractors.e: Default provider retention is limited (for example AWS CloudTrail Event history covers 90 days and the Azure Activity log is kept for 90 days); longer retention needs a trail, export or SIEM that you configure.

explanation.interview_angle: Engineering interviewers use this to see whether you think of IR readiness as logging, access and time, not only as tools.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
NIST SP 800-61r2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (superseded)

questions.question: True or false: at a bank, the incident lead adds two external DFIR consultants and extends the planned response window, then briefs the Chief Risk Officer on the incident. In NIST SP 800-61r3 terms, the first action is escalation and the briefing of the CRO is elevation.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: True. r3 (RS.MA-04, incidents are escalated or elevated as needed) distinguishes the two: escalation generally means increasing resources or time frames, while elevation means involving a higher level of management in the response. Adding external responders and more time is escalation; bringing in the CRO is elevation. Banks usually define both triggers in their severity matrix (for example which severity levels require senior management to be informed), so they are tracked separately in the incident record.

distractors.b: Many people use the two words interchangeably, which makes the statement look wrong. r3 separates them: more resources or time is escalation; involving higher management is elevation.

explanation.interview_angle: Checks the precise vocabulary that IR managers use in bank escalation matrices.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: An L1 analyst opened a Low-severity ticket: commodity malware quarantined on a workstation. You find that the workstation belongs to a payments operator with access to the payment initiation application, and proxy logs show beaconing to 203.0.113.50 every 60 seconds that started before the quarantine and continues from a second process. What do you do with the severity?

options.text: Keep it at Low: severity is fixed when the ticket is opened, so that SOC metrics stay comparable over time
Keep it at Low until a fraudulent payment is confirmed, then raise it
Raise it now per the severity matrix, record the facts behind the change, and escalate
Close the Low ticket and open a new High ticket so that the timeline starts cleanly

explanation.correct: Severity is reassessed whenever new facts change the picture. Two facts move it up here: the asset is critical for the bank (access to payment initiation means possible direct financial loss for the bank and its customers), and the activity is ongoing (beaconing continues from a second process, so the quarantine did not end the compromise; command and control over web protocols, T1071.001). NIST SP 800-61r3 asks responders to track and validate the status of all ongoing incidents so that those needing more resources or a different strategy are identified quickly (RS.MA-04). Record why the severity changed and keep the original ticket and timeline.

distractors.a: Metrics must not drive classification; under-classifying an active compromise on a payments workstation delays the response that limits customer and financial harm.
distractors.b: Waiting for a fraudulent payment means waiting for the very impact the response is meant to prevent.
distractors.d: A new ticket breaks the timeline and the audit trail of decisions, which you need for root-cause analysis and any regulatory report.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you treat severity as a living assessment and know what makes a bank asset critical.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3 - Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
MITRE ATT&CK T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols

questions.question: A bank's internet-banking service, which supports a critical function, is unavailable for 3 hours, and the incident lasts 30 hours until fully resolved. About 20,000 clients (4 % of the service's users) and about 3 % of the daily average transactions (by number and value) were affected; no clients or counterparts flagged as relevant were hit. No data was compromised, there was no media coverage or wave of complaints, only one Member State was affected, and costs are about 40,000 EUR. On these facts, is it a major incident under the DORA classification rules (Delegated Regulation 2024/1772)?

options.text: Yes: downtime over 2 hours and duration over 24 hours are two thresholds, which is enough once a critical service is affected
No: duration and service downtime are a single criterion, so only one materiality threshold is met
Yes: any incident that affects a critical service is automatically a major incident
No: under DORA only incidents that involve personal data can be classified as major

explanation.correct: Under Article 8 of Delegated Regulation 2024/1772, an incident is major when it has affected critical services and either the data-loss threshold for a successful, malicious and unauthorised access that may result in data losses is met (Article 9(5)(b)), or two or more of the other materiality thresholds in Article 9 are met. Article 9(3) defines one threshold for the criterion 'duration and service downtime': duration over 24 hours or downtime over 2 hours for services supporting critical or important functions. Here only that threshold is met; clients (over 10 % or over 100,000), transactions (over 10 % of the daily average), reputational impact, geographical spread (two or more Member States), data losses and economic impact (over 100,000 EUR) are not. Classification is not a one-off: complaints, media coverage or revised client counts can change the result, so reassess and document the basis of each decision.

distractors.a: The trap: Article 9(3) puts duration and downtime in one criterion, so meeting both still counts as a single threshold.
distractors.c: Affecting critical services is the precondition, not the whole test; it must be combined with the data-loss condition or with two other thresholds.
distractors.d: DORA covers ICT-related incidents in general; data losses are one criterion among several, and personal data is mainly a GDPR question.

explanation.interview_angle: Senior bank IR and risk roles are expected to read the DORA thresholds precisely rather than count headline numbers.

references.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 - classification of ICT-related incidents

questions.question: Another bank's CSIRT emails your bank's SOC: since 02:00, 198.51.100.10, one of your NAT egress addresses, has been scanning their internet-banking hosts on many ports. You have no alert of your own. What do you do first?

options.text: Close it: without an internal alert of your own, the report is most likely a misattribution or spam
Block the reporting bank's IP ranges at the perimeter firewall so that their complaint and any retaliation traffic stops
Shut down the bank's internet gateway until the source of the scanning has been found and removed
Verify the sender via a known contact, then map the address to the internal host with NAT and firewall logs

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 (RS.MA-02) tells organisations to have mechanisms for third parties to report incidents and to take such reports seriously, and gives this exact case: a party claiming that its systems are being attacked from a system at your organisation. Verify the reporter's identity through a known channel (the email itself could be a pretext), translate the public address to the internal host using NAT or firewall session logs for the reported window, and examine that host: process, user, EDR alerts, signs of compromise such as network service discovery (T1046) or an unauthorised scanner. Reply to the other bank through the agreed channel; coordination with peer organisations is part of incident communication.

distractors.a: The absence of an internal alert is a detection gap to investigate, not proof that the report is wrong; external reports are a normal source of incidents.
distractors.b: Blocking the reporter hides the symptom, damages a peer relationship and leaves a possibly compromised host inside your network.
distractors.c: Over-containment: cutting internet access stops a bank's customer-facing services for a problem that can probably be traced to one host in minutes.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you treat third-party reports as incident inputs and know how to map a public IP back to an internal host.

questions.question: A national CSIRT sends your MSSP a list of command-and-control domains marked TLP:AMBER+STRICT. An analyst wants to email the list to the SOC contacts of all 40 MSSP clients so they can block the domains. What does TLP 2.0 allow?

options.text: Not as planned: keep it inside the MSSP and ask the source for permission before passing it to clients
Sending it is fine, because TLP:AMBER always lets recipients share with their clients on a need-to-know basis
Sending it is fine if the TLP label is removed and the list is presented as the MSSP's own research
Sending it is fine, because TLP restricts only personal data and these are technical indicators

explanation.correct: In FIRST TLP 2.0, TLP:AMBER allows sharing within the recipient organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis, but TLP:AMBER+STRICT restricts sharing to the organisation only. A recipient who needs to share more widely than the label allows must get explicit permission from the source. The MSSP can work with the indicators internally and ask the CSIRT for permission, or for a version released at a wider label, to protect its clients.

distractors.b: That is the rule for plain TLP:AMBER, where clients are included by default. The +STRICT suffix removes clients from the sharing boundary.
distractors.c: Re-badging the data to escape its label breaks the source's sharing restriction and the trust that keeps the information flowing.
distractors.d: TLP sets sharing boundaries for any sensitive information, not only personal data; indicators can reveal the source's own investigation or its victims.

explanation.interview_angle: MSSP and CTI roles check that you know the AMBER versus AMBER+STRICT difference, where clients are the key boundary.

questions.question: A security vendor's detection engineer wants to load a new commercial IOC feed straight into the blocklist pushed to every customer firewall. Many entries are IP addresses with no first-seen date or confidence score, and some sit in large CDN and cloud-hosting ranges. What should come first?

options.text: Load every IP into blocking right away, because a false block is always safer than a missed attack
Drop the IP indicators entirely and keep only the file hashes, since hashes never cause false positives
Vet it: check age and confidence, drop shared-infrastructure IPs, and run it alert-only first
Block an IP only after it has been seen attacking the vendor's own network

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-150 says that before acting on threat information you confirm it is correct and relevant and understand the impact of acting versus not acting. IP indicators age quickly (attackers move infrastructure; the Pyramid of Pain rates IPs as easy for them to change), and an address in a shared CDN or cloud range can serve many legitimate sites, so blocking it can cause a customer outage. Running the feed in detect-only mode first shows its real hit and false-positive rate; then promote recent, high-confidence, non-shared indicators to blocking, with an expiry date.

distractors.a: Blocking a shared CDN or SaaS address can break business services for every customer at once; in a vendor product, that outage becomes your own incident.
distractors.b: Hashes are even easier for attackers to change than IPs, and feeds can contain wrong hashes too; the fix is vetting, not abandoning a whole indicator type.
distractors.d: That defeats the purpose of threat intelligence, which is to act on other organisations' observations before you are hit.

explanation.interview_angle: Vendor and engineering interviews probe whether you treat IOCs as perishable data with a false-positive cost.

questions.question: During triage you find an unknown executable in the Downloads folder of a finance team laptop. You want to know quickly whether it is known malware. What is the safest first use of public threat-intelligence services?

options.text: Upload the file to a public multi-engine scanner to get the most complete verdict
Compute its hash and look that up; if unknown, analyse it in an internal sandbox
Post the file on a public analyst forum so that the community can examine it
Run the file on your own analyst workstation and watch what it does

explanation.correct: A hash lookup tells you whether the sample is already known without disclosing it. Uploading the file to a public scanner makes it available to others: Microsoft's incident response guidance warns that many adversaries monitor submission counts on services like VirusTotal to learn that their targeted malware has been discovered, and the file may also contain your organisation's data or names. If the hash is unknown, detonate the file in an internal or private sandbox and keep the original as evidence. On Windows, Get-FileHash in PowerShell returns the SHA-256 by default.

distractors.a: It can tip off a targeted attacker who watches for uploads, and may leak internal data embedded in the file; check the hash first.
distractors.c: Same disclosure problem, and it may also break confidentiality rules for incident data.
distractors.d: Executing unknown code on an analyst machine can compromise that machine and the network, and undermines your evidence handling.

explanation.interview_angle: Simple but telling: it shows whether you think about operational security during triage.

questions.question: Your MSSP receives a vendor CTI report: a campaign used the domain upd-cdn.example.net and a scheduled task named 'OneDriveSyncCheck' between 1 and 21 September. It is now 14 October, and an analyst has added both indicators to the detection rules for all clients. What else is needed to know whether any client was hit?

options.text: Nothing more is needed: the new rules will raise an alert if either indicator ever shows up again
Search the last 24 hours of client logs, because activity older than that is no longer relevant
Email each client's security contact and ask whether their staff noticed anything unusual in September
Retro-hunt each client's DNS, proxy and endpoint logs over the campaign window, noting retention gaps

explanation.correct: Forward-looking rules only catch new use of the indicators; a compromise from September that has moved on to other infrastructure would never trigger them. Searching historical data over the whole campaign window, plus a margin before it, answers the actual question, in line with NIST SP 800-61r3's advice to look for indicators of compromise both on assets known to be targeted and on other potential targets (RS.AN-08). Where a client's log retention does not reach back to 1 September, the honest answer is 'unknown', and that gap is reported to the client. The scheduled-task indicator maps to T1053.005 and can be hunted in task-creation events (Event ID 4698) where they are collected.

distractors.a: Rules only see the future. If the campaign succeeded in September, the attacker may already use new domains and the rule stays silent.
distractors.b: The activity window is in September; a 24-hour search cannot find it.
distractors.c: Clients rarely notice a quiet intrusion; the evidence is in the logs the MSSP already holds.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you know the difference between adding a detection and retro-hunting, and say out loud when data is missing.

questions.question: A web shell is found on one of six internet-banking front-end servers behind a load balancer. The infrastructure team wants to rebuild that server from the gold image tonight and close the incident. As IR lead, what do you require before the scope can be called known?

options.text: Hunt the other front ends and linked systems for the same shell, IPs and persistence; review its use; preserve evidence first
Nothing more: the gold image is clean, so rebuilding removes the web shell and the incident is resolved once the server is back in the pool
Notify all internet-banking customers now that their accounts were compromised
Patch the web application on the affected server, then close the incident

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-61r3 calls determining an incident's magnitude one of the most challenging parts of incident response and recommends looking for indicators of compromise, persistence and other signs on assets known to be targeted and on other potential targets (RS.AN-08); doing it superficially lets the incident continue elsewhere unnoticed. Five identical servers share the same exposure (exploitation of a public-facing application, T1190), and a web shell (T1505.003) is often used to steal credentials or reach back-end systems, which would change the customer and regulatory impact. A rebuild is a valid eradication step, but only after the server's disk, memory and logs are preserved and you know where else to act.

distractors.b: Rebuilding one server removes one copy of the shell. If the attacker planted shells on the other five or used stolen credentials elsewhere, they stay in.
distractors.c: Customer notification needs evidence of what was accessed; announcing a compromise you have not scoped can be wrong and harmful. Assess the impact first, then decide with legal and compliance.
distractors.d: Patching the entry point on one host leaves the other five exposed and does nothing about what the attacker has already done.

explanation.interview_angle: Separates candidates who close tickets from those who own scope: 'where else?' is the point of the question.

questions.question: A newly formed SOC at a software company has time to write only three incident playbooks this quarter. Which approach follows NIST SP 800-61r3 guidance on procedures?

options.text: One playbook per ATT&CK tactic, starting with Reconnaissance and working down the matrix
Three playbooks for the most sophisticated nation-state scenarios, since everyday incidents can be handled from the analysts' experience
The most common incident types in your own history, plus one urgent emergency task such as rebuilding the identity platform
None until the first major incident shows which playbooks are really needed

explanation.correct: r3 notes that detailed procedures cannot cover every situation, so organisations should document responses to the most common types of incidents and threats, and also procedures for critical processes that may be urgently needed in an emergency, giving the example of redeploying the organisation's primary authentication platform. Playbooks format those procedures as actionable steps. Your own ticket history (phishing, account compromise, endpoint malware) tells you what is common; a rarely used but critical procedure is exactly what nobody remembers under pressure.

distractors.a: Tactics are not incident types; a Reconnaissance playbook is rarely actionable, and this order ignores where your incidents actually come from.
distractors.b: Rare scenarios matter, but most analyst hours go to common incidents; handling those without structure gives inconsistent results and no metrics.
distractors.d: Writing a playbook during a major incident is too late; r3 also notes that procedures can be tested or exercised to verify their accuracy and train staff, which needs them to exist first.

explanation.interview_angle: Engineering and SOAR interviews ask how you prioritise playbook work; data-driven plus critical emergencies is the expected answer.

questions.question: A bank's CISO office is organising a discussion-based tabletop exercise on a ransomware scenario to test the IR plan. Put the steps in order.

options.text: Hold the hotwash right after the discussion: what went well, where training is needed, which plan sections need updating
Define topic, scope, objectives and participants, including decision-makers from legal, compliance and communications
Write the after action report with observations and recommendations for the IR plan
Develop the material: scenario, facilitator guide with discussion questions, participant guide
Run the facilitated discussion while a data collector records observations
Assign action items and update the IR plan based on the report

explanation.correct: NIST SP 800-84 describes tabletop exercises as discussion-based events where a facilitator presents a scenario and asks questions about roles, coordination and decision-making, without deploying equipment. The sequence is: design the event (topic, scope, objectives, participants), develop the material, conduct the exercise with a data collector, hold the debrief (hotwash) immediately afterwards, capture observations and recommendations in the after action report, then assign action items and update the plan. For a bank, the scenario should force real decisions (taking payment systems offline, whether the incident may be major and reportable, what to tell customers), which is why legal, compliance and communications must be in the room; NIST SP 800-61r3 lists exercise findings as an input to improvement (ID.IM-02).
explanation.interview_angle: Governance roles run these exercises; knowing that the output is a tracked plan update, not just a meeting, is the point.

questions.question: In a bank's ransomware tabletop, the playbook says 'isolate the payment-processing servers on confirmed encryption', but the business continuity plan assumes those servers stay online, and nobody in the room can say who may approve taking them offline at 02:00. What is the right corrective action?

options.text: Let the on-shift SOC analyst decide at the time, because speed matters more than approval
Name who may take payment services offline (and a deputy), under which criteria, align the BCP with it and re-test
Remove isolation from the playbook for payment servers, because in banking availability always comes first
Leave both plans unchanged, since real incidents differ too much from exercises to agree decision rights in advance

explanation.correct: Taking a critical service offline is a business decision with customer, financial and regulatory consequences, so the authority to make it and the criteria for using it must be agreed before the incident. NIST SP 800-61r3 asks that individuals with incident response duties be given the authority they need (GV.RR-02) and that business continuity plans be synchronised with incident response plans (ID.IM-04). Microsoft's incident response planning checklist lists 'who has authority to shut down mission-critical workloads?' among the decisions to settle before an attack. Encryption spreading across payment servers (T1486) can turn a contained incident into days of outage; the plan must say who decides, on what evidence, and what the continuity workaround is.

distractors.a: Speed matters, but an analyst cannot weigh payment-system downtime against customer and regulatory impact, and a contested decision at 02:00 costs more time than a pre-agreed one.
distractors.c: Ruling out containment for the most critical systems invites the worst outcome: encrypted payment servers are unavailable too, and for much longer.
distractors.d: Exercises exist to find exactly this gap; the decision owner and criteria can be agreed even if real scenarios differ in detail.

explanation.interview_angle: Senior bank roles are judged on spotting decision-rights gaps and fixing them in the plan, not on technical steps.

questions.question: Evidence shows the attacker holds a Domain Admin account and can read executives' mailboxes. The incident team has been coordinating through the corporate chat and email, which run on the same identity platform. What should change?

options.text: Keep using the current channels, but mark every incident message 'CONFIDENTIAL' in the subject line
Create a new private chat channel in the same tenant, restricted to the IR team members
Stop all incident communication until containment is complete, so that nothing can leak
Move to a pre-arranged out-of-band channel outside the compromised identity and mail systems

explanation.correct: With domain-level privileges and mailbox access (T1078.002, T1114), the attacker may read the response plan in real time and adapt, or lock responders out. Microsoft's incident response planning guidance asks teams to prepare out-of-band communications for exactly these cases (email and collaboration services impaired, documentation repositories ransomed, phone numbers unavailable) and to keep key information such as contacts and procedures stored offline. NIST SP 800-61r2 already recommended multiple, separate communication mechanisms, including out-of-band methods. Set this up during preparation; improvising it mid-incident is slow and leaky.

distractors.a: A label does not stop someone who can read the mailbox; it may even highlight what to read.
distractors.b: A new channel in the same tenant is still governed by the identity platform the attacker administers.
distractors.c: Response depends on coordination; going silent delays containment. The fix is a safe channel, not no channel.

explanation.interview_angle: Checks that you think about the attacker watching the defenders, a common blind spot in junior answers.

questions.question: During a major incident the network team blocks an IP, the server team reboots a suspect host, nobody updates management, and no one records which actions were taken when. What is the first organisational fix?

options.text: Designate an incident lead who coordinates all actions, with a communications liaison and a recorder
Let each team carry on independently and ask every team for a written summary once the incident is over
Hand coordination of the response to the legal department, since the incident may lead to litigation
Pause the response until a full root-cause analysis shows which team should own the incident

explanation.correct: Uncoordinated actions destroy evidence (the reboot wiped memory), can tip off the attacker and leave gaps. NIST SP 800-61r3 suggests designating an incident lead for each incident (RS.MA-01) and recording the actions performed during an investigation while preserving the integrity of those records (RS.AN-06). Microsoft's incident response planning guidance describes matching roles: a technical incident leader, a communications liaison who keeps management (and third parties such as regulators) informed so the leader can stay focused, and an incident recorder. Every containment action then goes through one decision point and lands in one log.

distractors.b: Summaries written afterwards are incomplete and cannot replace a time-stamped record; meanwhile teams keep undoing each other's work.
distractors.c: Legal advises on privilege, notification and law enforcement, but does not run technical coordination.
distractors.d: Root cause comes out of the investigation; pausing the response to find it first lets the attacker carry on.

explanation.interview_angle: A behavioural-technical blend: interviewers want to hear the roles (lead, communications, scribe) and why the reboot was a problem.

questions.question: At 03:00 an MSSP analyst sees on a client's file server 'vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet' run by an admin account created 20 minutes earlier, followed by SMB connections from that server to 30 hosts. The contract lets the MSSP isolate endpoints through EDR; disabling accounts needs client approval. The client's on-call contact does not answer the first call. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Disable the new admin account in the client's directory anyway, because the emergency justifies acting
Wait until business hours, since the on-call contact did not pick up the phone
Isolate the affected hosts through EDR, keep working the escalation list, and log each action
Email the client a description of the alert and take no action until they reply

explanation.correct: Deleting volume shadow copies (T1490, inhibit system recovery) from a freshly created admin account and then fanning out over SMB is a typical ransomware precursor, so waiting is not an option. NIST SP 800-61r3 notes that a service provider's responsibilities, including its authority to act on the organisation's behalf and the restrictions on what it may do, should be defined in the contract. Use the authority you have (EDR isolation of the file server and of hosts showing the same activity), keep escalating through the client's contact list until a decision-maker approves the account action, and document every step with timestamps.

distractors.a: Acting outside the contract, however well meant, can break the client's processes, create liability and damage trust; get approval through the escalation path while using the actions you are allowed.
distractors.b: A ransomware precursor at 03:00 can encrypt the estate before business hours; an unanswered first call means moving to the next contact, not stopping.
distractors.d: Email alone is too slow for an active precursor, and doing nothing ignores the containment authority the contract already gives.

explanation.interview_angle: MSSP interviews test whether you act decisively within contractual authority and escalate for the rest.

questions.question: An 'impossible travel' alert fires for a developer at a software company: a successful sign-in from Bucharest, then 20 minutes later another from Frankfurt. Which first check most often explains this kind of alert?

options.text: Whether either IP is the company VPN, a proxy, or a cloud or mobile network
Whether the developer holds administrator rights in the production environment
Whether Germany appears on the company's list of high-risk countries for sign-ins
Whether the developer's password was changed within the last 90 days

explanation.correct: IP geolocation shows where the network egress point is, not where the person is. Corporate VPN concentrators, secure web gateways, cloud services and mobile carriers often place a user's traffic in another city or country, which is the most common benign cause of impossible-travel alerts. Check both IPs against your known egress ranges and compare the device and user agent of each sign-in in the identity provider's sign-in logs; if the second sign-in comes from an unknown network or a different device, treat it as a possible account compromise (T1078.004).

distractors.b: Admin rights raise the impact if the account is compromised, so they matter for severity, but they do not tell you whether the alert is true.
distractors.c: A country list validates nothing; both locations are in the EU, and the question is whether the user was really there.
distractors.d: Password age says nothing about whether this particular sign-in was legitimate.

explanation.interview_angle: A staple L1 question: validate the alert's assumption (IP location equals user location) before escalating.
